articles.title_orig: Nasdaq falls 1% as AI trade stumbles following OpenAI revenue setback
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq falls 1% as AI trade stumbles following OpenAI revenue setback
articles.content_orig:
The Nasdaq Composite slid on Thursday as new details about OpenAI spooked investors, putting the artificial intelligence trade under pressure.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq was down 1.25% to close at 27,193.34, while the S&P 500 declined 0.47% to 7,765.36. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 51.77 points, or 0.1%, to end at 51,231.64.
Shares of key tech names came under pressure after OpenAI's annualized revenue was revealed to be short of the amount previously signaled. Shares of Oracle were down more than 5%, while chipmakers such as Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices lost nearly 3% and almost 4%, respectively.
Adding to the downbeat sentiment, oil prices spiked also after President Donald Trump said he doesn't want to make a deal with Iran to end the war, while the U.S. is reportedly preparing for " massive bombing " in the Middle East. However, he later said that the U.S. won't attack Iran before the midterm elections early next month, moving oil off its highs. Brent crude was up 4.07% to $104.28 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate futures , meanwhile, advanced 3.64% to settle at $91.49.
Traders also watched the moves in rates after the 10-year Treasury yield and 30-year yield scaled to fresh 24-year highs this week. The benchmark 10-year yield was last down 5 basis points at 5.227%, while the 30-year yield was down 6 basis points at 5.601%. Those moves came after a solid 30-year auction by the Treasury .
"At the end of the day, I think it's inflation pressures, primarily driven by energy, that have shifted the Fed's disposition and have in a lot of ways shifted the long end of the curve as well," said Ross Mayfield, Baird investment strategist. "If we announced a deal with Iran tomorrow that was structurally sound and removed a lot of the tensions from the area, and oil dropped from $90 a barrel to $70 a barrel, yields would come down meaningfully."
Yields and oil have stoked volatility in equities of late, as concern grows that higher energy prices will keep inflation elevated and force the Federal Reserve to further raise rates.
While Mayfield said equities have been "pretty resilient" overall in the face of these pressures, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq notching fresh all-time highs this week, he still doesn't think it would "take much of a move higher" on the long end of the yield curve to spell "more significant headwinds" for stocks. He believes yields could stabilize in the 5% to 6% range.
"We are in the process of the market adjusting to these new yields," he added. "In a lot of ways, higher yields are reflective of stronger nominal growth and slightly higher inflation, and if that's the case going forward, then again, it makes the argument that this kind of higher-for-longer or normal-for-longer rate environment is probably here to stay, barring a big recession where the Fed cuts rates to zero."
Palantir Technologies was one of the few stocks that closed higher on Thursday, with shares gaining 2% after the name received an upgrade at Goldman Sachs . The firm called for more upside ahead as the total addressable market could be "setting up for another step function change" as a result of the shift to sovereign AI and bespoke applications.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite finished Thursday's session lower.
The broad market index and tech-heavy Nasdaq lost 0.47% and 1.25% to 7,765.36 and 27,193.34, respectively.
However, the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 51.77 points, or 0.1%, to 51,231.64.
OpenAI's revenue disappointed investors on Thursday, sending stocks related to artificial intelligence lower. But Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, is still optimistic on the trade.
"I am not concerned about OpenAI just tripling its revenue this year," he told CNBC. "They have actually had an acceleration in growth this quarter and are catching up to Anthropic in the enterprise business. These two companies combined are at around $120b of revenue run rate from nearly zero two years ago. That represents companies and consumers spending on AI, which is very promising."
"Companies and consumers are using AI and willing to pay for it," he also said. "That will ultimately drive everything else."
The 30-year Treasury auction on Thursday was not as strong as Wednesday's 10-year sale, putting yield at their highest level in decades, said Tony Miano, global investment strategy analyst at Wells Fargo Investment Institute.
Thursday's auction stopped at a high yield of 5.618%, up 31 basis points from the 5.308% result at the September auction, he noted.
Both the 10-year and 30-year sales show demand isn't broken, but it is concentrated at the front and belly of the curve,  Miano said.
"The long end is where investors are demanding the most compensation, consistent with a term-premium/duration-risk story rather than an outright 'no buyers' story," he added. "Net takeaway: today's 30-year result is a curve-steepening signal — long-duration paper absorbing the brunt of the repricing."
St. Louis Federal Reserve President Alberto Musalem joined the chorus of central bank officials who expect higher benchmark interest rates to stop energy price-induced inflation from causing wider economic damage.
"At this point in time, it's important to contain any further broadening of inflation pressures or any second-round effects, which could be coming from the negative supply shocks or the persistent demand pressures," the central banker said Thursday at a Bloomberg News conference. "To bring inflation back to target in a timely manner, more monetary policy firming will be required."
Like his colleagues, Musalem did not specify the degree of potential hikes, though he envisions a time frame of about 18 months during which he expects the bank to act to bring inflation back to the Fed's 2% target.
Musalem does not get a vote on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee until 2028, though he still provides input at meetings.
Bitcoin mining stocks tumbled as a pullback in the price of the flagship cryptocurrency amid the broader market sell-off. A Financial Times report that OpenAI's annualized revenue is about $20 billion less than what it previously signaled pressured the sector.
So called hybrid miners underperformed the broader crypto complex as investors reassessed their earnings and capital-intensive AI/data-center ambitions. Cipher Digital and Hut 8 dropped 10% each, while Terawulf slid 8%. Riot Platforms , which signed a compute and data center agreement with Anthropic earlier this year, lost 11%.
Pure play bitcoin miners Mara Holdings and CleanSpark declined 6% and 9%, respectively. Coinbase and Strategy were down about 3% each.
Oil prices stood off their highs of the day on Thursday after President Donald Trump said in a post on Truth Social that the U.S. "will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections" on Nov. 3.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures were last up 3.15% at $91.06 per barrel, while international benchmark Brent crude futures were 3.48% higher at $103.69 per barrel.
— Sean Conlon and Luke Fountain
Rosenblatt started covering cloud provider Nebius on Wednesday, setting a price target of $304 for the stock along with a buy rating. Shares closed Wednesday at $237.15.
The investment bank sees the company's revenues increasing along with its computing volumes, which are expected to rise to between 4.25 and 4.75 gigawatts of active power by 2030.
"Nebius is indeed is experiencing hypergrowth, with 2Q26 revenues up 5.5x Y/Y and 2026 total revenues expected to grow 6.5x--we forecast a revenue CAGR of 98% from FY2026 through FY2030," John McPeake at Rosenblatt on Wednesday.
Coffee franchise Starbucks has looked into buying restaurant chain Chipotle in a potential deal that would be the biggest restaurant acquisition of all time, the Financial Times reported on Thursday .
Chipotle's market capitalization is $39 billion, which would make a takeover more than triple the size of Burger King's $11.4bn purchase of Canadi

articles.title_orig: At least 30 dead in Russian bus strike as Moscow closes in on Ukraine’s ‘fortress belt’
articles.title_zh: At least 30 dead in Russian bus strike as Moscow closes in on Ukraine’s ‘fortress belt’
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv's allies needed to take "concrete action"
At least 30 people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the eastern front line city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials say.
Authorities said three people were also killed in the village of Bilenke, part of the Kramatorsk community.
Another 18 people were wounded, said Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin, accusing Russia of targeting buses carrying passengers to kill as many civilians as possible.
Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk are part of a so-called fortress belt that Moscow is trying to seize as part of Russian President Vladimir Putin's claim to the entire Ukrainian industrial region of Donbas.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said: "This strike will not go without our response."
In a post on Telegram, he said: "Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this. React harshly - exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have caused."
Images posted by local prosecutors showed the burning metal shell of the bus along with debris and some of the victims on the road.
Moscow is yet to comment on the latest attack. It follows a dramatic surge in Russian attacks across Ukraine and a heavy increase in civilian casualties.
According to the UN, Ukraine saw more civilians killed by August this year than were killed in all of 2025.
In one single attack that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky east of Kyiv early on Wednesday, 22 people were killed, including five children. Three of the children were only one year old.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who together with Zelensky visited the site of the Russian strike in Pryluky, said the attack showed Putin's "evil intent and evil strategy".
He announced "more sanctions on Russia, on the war machine of Putin, on the shadow fleet, on the oil companies, on the crypto, on the financing of the war" and told Zelensky the UK would stand with Ukraine "as long as it takes for you to prevail in this conflict".
After the deadly attack on Kramatorsk, Filashkin appealed to anyone who was still in the eastern front line region to move to safer parts of Ukraine.
Given the sharp deterioration of security in the two neighbouring cities, he said all public transport had been ordered to stop. The safety of civilians was paramount, and "we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers", he said.
Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine launched by Putin in 2022 - a claim rejected by Ukraine and its allies as baseless.
Donbas is made up of two regions - Luhansk and Donetsk - and with most of Luhansk under Russian control, the Kremlin is also aiming to capture remaining 20% of Donetsk territory still held by Ukraine.
For much of the war Kramatorsk acted as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military, however it has now come under almost daily Russian attack as its military moves closer to the east of the city.
Glide bombs in particular have been launched at Slovyansk and Kramatorsk. The bombs are fitted with winglets so they glide towards their target rather than simply fall.  In late August as many as nine glide bombs were fired at Kramatorsk in one day.
Kramatorsk city council described the strike as a "horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population".
"Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets," it said.
Children killed while they slept as Russian missile kills 22 in block of flats
Civilians told to flee Ukraine's fortress cities as Russia bids to control Donbas
Russia has in recent weeks been launching constant air raids on the capital Kyiv, with sirens ringing virtually non-stop.
On Thursday, Kyiv police said four people were killed and two injured in the latest Russian attack on the city.
The attacks are forcing schoolchildren out of classes into underground shelters, shuttering businesses, and disrupting public transport.
Moscow's strikes on Ukraine's key infrastructure, particularly on its energy grid, are causing power outages already and are even affecting the water supply. Local water authorities in the capital warned on Thursday that pressure was dropping across the city's right bank due to power cuts.
Kyiv's metro network - which millions of residents rely on - on Thursday briefly halted all its train traffic due to a voltage drop from "external power centres". Trains later started moving again - but at greater intervals, local officials said.
Zelensky offered his condolences to families and loved ones affected by the latest attack and said Ukraine's partners needed to provide "concrete action through new defence packages for the protection of Ukraine".
Ahead of the Pryluky attack, the Ukrainian leader had warned this week of intelligence suggesting plans for a major Russian onslaught, and in Kyiv families responded by heading to metro stations for shelter.
Such warnings are for now one of the only defences Ukrainians have.
Interceptor missiles are in short supply around the world, so Ukraine has little  chance to stop incoming Russian ballistics.
Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses.
On Thursday, Russian state-run media reported that a number of websites in the country were inaccessible following a Ukrainian drone attack on a data centre of Yandex - Russia's largest search engine.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Isaias live updates: Gulf Coast braces for dangerous storm
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias live updates: Gulf Coast braces for dangerous storm
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Mandatory evacuations have been announced and schools closed across parts of coastal Florida after Isaias intensified into the Atlantic season's first hurricane , advancing towards the US Gulf Coast Thursday, the National Hurricane Center said.
Forecasters warned that Isaias could deliver destructive hurricane-force winds to the Florida Panhandle, alongside southern Alabama and southern Mississippi.
“A life-threatening storm surge is expected from the Mouth of the Mississippi River to Suwannee, Florida. Residents in the warning area should follow advice given by local officials and evacuate immediately if told to do so,” the National Weather Service said Thursday.
“Damaging wind gusts are possible over much of central and northern Alabama and portions of western and northern Georgia, especially in areas of higher terrain,’ the NWS continued.
It could also cause a life-threatening storm surge along areas of the northern Gulf Coast, while potentially bringing heavy rains of 3 to 7 inches (7 to 18 centimeters) across the central Gulf Coast, according to the hurricane center.
An advisory from the Miami-based hurricane center said the cyclone’s center was positioned approximately 740 kilometres (460 miles) south-southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi River , carrying maximum sustained winds of around 121 kph (75 mph).
After the storm initially formed earlier Wednesday in the warm waters of eastern Mexico, communities in its potential path moved quickly to prepare with landfall forecast as soon as Friday evening.
Some Gulf oil wells paused production, and at least four Florida school districts canceled classes for later in the week while Okaloosa County announced mandatory evacuations for some coastal areas. Governors in Florida and Alabama declared a state of emergency for dozens of counties.
The National Weather Service told communities from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to Gulf County, Florida, to prepare for the possibility of “long-duration power outages.”
Isaias is developing more than four months into the Atlantic hurricane season, nearly tying a 121-year-old record for the area’s latest-forming hurricane. According to the National Weather Service, the record dates to 1905, when the year’s first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.
The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over that ocean. Storm activity has been above average in the Pacific, where Tropical Storm Simon formed Wednesday off Mexico.
Isaias is expected to strike along a wide swath of coastline that’s very familiar with major hurricanes.
One of the 20th century’s worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Mississippi, in 1969. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 razed neighborhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael leveled homes and buildings near Panama City, Florida, in 2018.
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15 per cent of crude pumped annually in the U.S.
As of Wednesday about 25 per cent of the oil production in the region was temporarily halted, taking about 511,000 barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said eight of the Gulf's 371 manned oil platforms were evacuated.
With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.
As it moves inland, Isaias might also disrupt Saturday’s college football showdown between rivals Georgia and Alabama, a game President Donald Trump has planned to attend.
In Alabama, the cities of Gulf Shores and Orange Beach issued a statement encouraging people in low-lying areas to voluntarily evacuate.
Gulf Shores resident Maranie Adams gathered water and other supplies as her family moved belongings, including a hot tub motor, to higher ground. Her family planned to ride out the storm at home, roughly a half-mile from shore, sheltering indoors alongside their flock of chickens.
“We’re having to get crates to bring them into the house so they don’t blow away,” Adams said. “It’s going to be noisy.”
Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties, while Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared one for 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Bend regions. The state also planned to deploy a Miami-based urban search and rescue task force.
In Pensacola, electric utilities were pre-positioning crews to quickly repair any power outages. City officials provided sand for residents to fill sandbags to protect their homes against flooding. And Mayor D.C. Reeves urged people to check on older adult neighbors and others who might need help.
“Obviously no need to panic at this point,” Reeves told a news conference. “This is really about preparation.”

articles.title_orig: US investigates 9 universities over alleged visa fraud, with focus on China
articles.title_zh: US investigates 9 universities over alleged visa fraud, with focus on China
articles.content_orig:
Stanford and Brown are among schools facing scrutiny over alleged visa abuse and Chinese influence on federally funded research
The Trump administration is launching an investigation into nine US universities over alleged J-1 visa fraud, with officials raising concerns about Chinese scholars and the Chinese government.
At a Thursday press conference, Anthony D’Esposito, inspector general of the US Department of Labor, announced what he called a “historic investigation” into J-1 visa fraud at Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown, the University of Pittsburgh, UC Davis, Caltech, Arizona State University and MIT. Subpoenas have been issued to the universities, officials said.

articles.title_orig: China breakthrough may push sustainable jet fuel gross profit margin past 50%
articles.title_zh: China breakthrough may push sustainable jet fuel gross profit margin past 50%
articles.content_orig:
Biomass-to-jet fuel conversion method could boost production and help meet global aviation industry’s net-zero carbon goals, researchers say
Chinese researchers have developed a catalyst that converts synthesis gas into sustainable jet fuel – a breakthrough that could boost production, help meet net-zero carbon goals and yield a gross profit margin exceeding 50 per cent.
Based on a techno-economic analysis that modelled a planned 100,000-tonnes-per-year jet fuel plant, the researchers estimated they could achieve a gross profit margin surpassing 50 per cent.
“The excellent pilot test results and the positive techno-economic and life-cycle assessments underscore its strong potential for industrial deployment,” the team said in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Communications in September.

articles.title_orig: European industry groups call for urgent EU action on China trade
articles.title_zh: European industry groups call for urgent EU action on China trade
articles.content_orig:
By ELIANA SILVER, SENIOR FOREIGN NEWS REPORTER
Published: 06:17 EDT, 8 October 2026 | Updated: 06:22 EDT, 8 October 2026
The EU and China are edging closer to a trade war, with the bloc’s commerce chief warning that its trade deficit with China is ‘unsustainable’ as he began two days of talks in Beijing aimed at averting an escalating confrontation.
Beijing, meanwhile, hit back by warning that Europe lacks the capacity to wage a trade war, issuing a blunt challenge: ‘Let them try.’
Writing on X on Thursday, European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic said: 'Day one in China, with one goal: begin rebalancing our... unsustainable trade deficit.'
'I started by hearing directly from EU businesses here. The message around the table was clear: the need to improve access to the Chinese market, while boosting our economic security,' he added.
Last year, every day, China exported to the EU around a billion euros more in goods and services than went the other way, according to European figures.
Many in Europe blame this on unfair trade practices by Beijing, including state subsidies and price dumping, undercutting European rivals in industries from cars to chemicals.
The Asian giant could throttle supplies of items such as rare earth minerals that are vital for the continent's industrial sector – or throw up barriers to European exports to China.
The two days of discussions by Mr Sefcovic in Beijing come as France and Germany, the bloc's two biggest powers, threaten to up the ante.
Last year, every day, China exported to the EU around a billion euros more in goods and services than went the other way, according to European figures (pictured: Xi Jinping)
In a letter earlier this week, President Emmanuel Macron and Chancellor Friedrich Merz called for a 'credible instrument' to respond quickly to any escalation by Beijing
In a letter earlier this week, President Emmanuel Macron and Chancellor Friedrich Merz called for a 'credible instrument' to respond quickly to any escalation by Beijing.
The proposed weapon – to be discussed at an EU leaders' summit next week – would give the European Commission the power to respond to a trade aggression within days.
Among other actions, it proposed making it easier for the European Commission to use the bloc's so-called 'trade bazooka', the Anti-Coercion Instrument.
This is a never-used-before raft of measures for blocking or restricting trade and investment from countries found to be putting undue pressure on EU member nations or corporations.
Yet not all EU nations agree on such tough measures. Spain, the eurozone's fourth-largest economy, has been less adversarial toward China in recent years.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has visited Beijing four times in three years. Far-Right and Left-wing lawmakers from Ireland to Bulgaria formed an unusual coalition on Wednesday to vote against resolution calling for tougher China policies.
China immediately warned Paris and Berlin on Tuesday against 'protectionist' measures.
'They should avoid going down the wrong path in the wrong way, only to ultimately suffer the consequences themselves,' the commerce ministry said in a statement.
And an editorial in China's state run Global Times newspaper read: 'The EU does not have the capacity to wage a trade war against China. If it is truly determined to do so, then let it try.'
China's foreign ministry said Thursday that Beijing hopes that it can work with Brussels 'in the same direction and address each other's concerns through dialogue and consultation'.
'As a principle, China has always believed that adhering to openness and cooperation and resolving economic and trade differences through equal dialogue and consultation is in the common interests of both China and the EU,' spokesman Mao Ning told a regular briefing.
The stakes are also high for President Xi Jinping, however, with China heavily reliant on exports in order to compensate for its stuttering domestic economy.
The EU parliament's trade committee chief, Bernd Lange, said ahead of Mr Sefcovic's trip that this 'economic crisis in China' gives the bloc 'bargaining power'.
'The EU has a well-supplied toolbox to counter unfair subsidies, dumping, discriminatory procurement, and economic coercion. These instruments must be applied consistently and, where necessary, enhanced,' Mr Lange said in a statement.
EU and Chinese officials have been negotiating since June, and Mr Sefcovic raised hopes earlier this year when he said that he wanted 'tangible results by October'.
Mr Sefcovic has identified three priorities: addressing surging imports in strategically important sectors, increasing European exports to China and improving access to critical raw materials.
The EU is also seeking clearer export-licensing arrangements for rare earths and other materials after China introduced restrictions last year.
Brussels hopes to manage Chinese exports through voluntary limits, for example on hybrid cars shipped to the bloc. Beijing, though, firmly opposes import quotas.
Analysts are cautious about the prospects for a broad agreement being struck this week.
Maros Sefcovic said: 'Day one in China, with one goal: begin rebalancing our... unsustainable trade deficit'
The EU imports sizable amounts of Chinese lithium-ion batteries and hybrid electric vehicles (Pictured: Workers produce transmissions for new energy vehicles in Wuhu)
Workers use machinery to dig at a rare earth mine in Ganxian county in central China's Jiangxi province
'But if one sector could be identified in which an export-restraint agreement with China could be tested, that would be a good step,' Ignacio Garcia Bercero, from Brussels think-tank Bruegel, said.
Zhu Tian, economics professor at Shanghai's China Europe International Business School, agreed, saying that the talks could yield agreements 'on some specific issues'.
Politicians and economists across the 27-nation bloc consider China's massive subsidies and exports a major threat to core industrial sectors from steel foundries to car factories.
China diverted many of its exports to the EU and other markets after the US raised tariffs.
In a debate Tuesday in European Parliament in Strasbourg, lawmakers overwhelmingly expressed anxiety alongside defiance over trade with China.
On Wednesday, they voted 454 to 86 on a resolution to toughen up on China that centered on a call for 'economic reciprocity and a proportionate EU response if China does not open its markets'.
Ahead of the vote, Hilde Vautmans, the Belgian lawmaker who led the resolution, said that 'Europe has economic power, it's time we used it.'
Despite the seeming European unity this week, it remains unclear what the EU can or is willing to do. It has already rolled out trade measures against Chinese steel imports and e-commerce small parcels.
France's High Commission for Strategy and Planning in February called for swift action, like 30 per cent tariffs on many of China's exports, and a devaluation of the euro against the Chinese currency.
Sales of German autos are plummeting in China but China is also poised to gobble up market share in Europe by undercutting European automakers on price thanks to heavy state subsidies.
There have already been mass layoffs at major manufacturers like Volkswagen.
The European Policy Centre in Brussels said in June that European battery producers, solar panels, steel, electric vehicles, chemicals and machinery are already haemorrhaging jobs and capacity and called for a trade investigative body modelled on Section 301 of the US Trade Act.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the phenomenon another 'China shock' for Europe, similar to what happened in the U.S. in the early 2000s when hundreds of thousands of factory jobs in the American heartland were wiped out.
The EU's ailing economy requires both a domestic overhaul and a more aggressive foreign trade policy, especially with China, said Tim Rühlig, a China analyst at the European Union I

articles.title_orig: Catherine Zeta-Jones shocks with sassy response for having read husband Michael Douglas's book
articles.title_zh: Catherine Zeta-Jones shocks with sassy response for having read husband Michael Douglas's book
articles.content_orig:
By REBECCA LAWRENCE, DEPUTY SHOWBUSINESS EDITOR (DIGITAL FEATURES)
Published: 07:04 EDT, 8 October 2026 | Updated: 12:57 EDT, 8 October 2026
Michael Douglas has revealed how wife Catherine Zeta-Jones tamed his womanising ways.
The Hollywood Lothario had quite the reputation as a ladies man, indulging in at least five on-set flings and countless affairs.
Yet everything changed when he fell in love with Catherine the second he saw her in 1998's The Mask of Zorro.
Initially worried that their 25-year age gap would make their romance a non-starter, Michael was delighted to read in an interview that she preferred to date older men, and set up a meeting at the Deauville film festival.
The pair were joined by Catherine's Zorro co-star Antonio Banderas and his wife Melanie Griffith for dinner and drinks, with Catherine later returning for drinks one on one.
After a night spent talking, Michael – who was in the midst of divorcing Diandra Luker at the time – shared: 'In a moment of temporary insanity, I blurted out: "I’m going to be the father of your children".'
It was a declaration that turned out to be true, but not until Catherine had imposed her boundaries and ensured he would remain faithful.
Michael Douglas has revealed Catherine Zeta-Jones tamed his womanising ways after making him wait nine months to sleep together (pictured in 1999)
Her first tactic was to take things slow with Michael, refraining from sleeping together after their dates.
Michael recalled that whenever he would offer to take her home she would claim to have a family member or friend in the area who could give her a lift.
'Totally smitten', Michael didn't notice the pattern at first until 'it finally dawned on me. She wanted to take it slow.'
Yet Michael did all that he could to spend time with her, coordinating schedules and flying out to meet her, but still, he noted there was ' still nothing physical between us'.
He recalled: ' I looked forward to seeing her whenever I could. It wasn't that often, but I drank up every moment. What started as the two of us getting to know each other slowly turned into the longest courtship I had ever undertaken!
'I had always been inclined to slip right into physical intimacy, but with Catherine, I was willing to take whatever time we both needed.'
He added: 'As Catherine said, I didn't want her to become just another ex-girlfriend on my list, and she didn't want Michael Douglas to become just another ex-boyfriend on hers.
Michael revealed the 'little things' kept him going, such as notes she would send him and their little conversations.
However, he did also later confess to sleeping with five different women at the time he was courting Catherine.
Michael's luck changed in June 1999 when he invited Catherine to stay at his holiday home in Mallorca, promising her the use of her own bedroom.
He invited his friend Pat Riley, President of the Miami Heat, and Pat's wife of 30 years Chris to stay with them the same time because he wanted Catherine to see him with a 'normal, stable couple'.
The Hollywood Lothario had quite the reputation as a ladies man, indulging in countless affairs. Yet everything changed when he fell in love with Catherine (pictured together in 2024)
Michael explained: 'That, I hoped, would offset my 'reputation' that Catherine had mentioned the first night we met. This was important to me. Catherine was very important to me.
'And I thought that having my treasured friends around would help Catherine feel comfortable. Turns out, I was right.'
He then revealed that during the visit the pair slept together for the first time and agreed to make things official, although Catherine insisted she would only date him if he was monogamous – prompting Douglas to make 'five quick calls'.
Michael explained: 'Just after my marriage, I had been seeing five other women. They knew I was recently separated and in the process of getting a divorce.
'I made sure they all lived in different cities, which felt like a respectful way to be nonmonogamous. None of them asked for a commitment or even asked what else I was up to.
'I am sure they were seeing other people, too. That day, I called each one to say I'd met somebody and would no longer be able to continue seeing them. They all took it well.'
Michael and Catherine then contacted their parents to announce they were seeing each other, with Kirk Douglas telling Michael he was a ' lucky b*****d'.
Catherine's parents were also on board with the romance, despite being younger than Michael, because they had been to see Kirk's film Spartacus for their first date.
Six months after making things official Catherine fell pregnant with their son Dylan, and on New Year's Eve 1999, despite both suffering from flu at the time, Michael popped the question in Aspen.
The couple tied the knot at the Plaza Hotel in New York City in November just three months after Dylan was born, in front of a crowd that included Bonnie Tyler, Tom Hanks, Whoopi Goldberg and Anthony Hopkins.
Michael's then-21-year-old son Cameron - from his previous marriage to Diandra - served as the best man.
After the wedding, and a romantic honeymoon in Aspen, the pair made an agreement that only one of them would work at a time to retain a sense of 'normality' for their son.
Michael opted to stay home after Catherine was offered her role in Chicago, explaining: 'While I was nowhere near ready to retire, I had carved out my career already. I had accomplished everything I wanted to do in films and had nothing left to prove.
'I was fine taking a stay-at-home role while Catherine's career continued to blossom. I knew how talented she was, and I knew how successful she would be. It was her time.'
It was a decision that paid off, with Catherine winning an Oscar for the role. The following year she gave birth to daughter Carys.
The couple tied the knot in 2000 and went on to welcome son Dylan and daughter Carys (pictured in 2011). They will celebrate their 26th wedding anniversary next month
They continued their pact until tragedy struck in 2010 when Michael was diagnosed with stage 4 tongue cancer, which he was thankfully able to beat.
In August 2013, Catherine confirmed that the couple were 'taking some time apart to evaluate and work on their marriage'.
The separation came two months after Michael blamed developing throat cancer on oral sex. His publicist later retracted the remarks and Michael said he 'regretted the embarrassment' they reportedly caused his wife.
Detailing their separation in his memoir, Michael penned: 'From the second we separated, I never gave up hope that we would reconcile. I love Catherine in a way that I have never loved any other woman.
'She’s my wife, my best friend, and my life partner. I could never lose her.'
The couple were back together within a year.
Yet when questioned how 'he won her back', this week, Michael snapped back to The Sunday Times: 'What, I won her back? It was a mutual… You know, we had our problems but I love her dearly and, 25 years, you know.
'Marriage is a lot of work, you know. And so, you know, we’re good. We’re in good shape. It’s all I can say.'
The pair will celebrate their 26th wedding anniversary next month.
Prior to meeting Catherine, Michael had several flings.
Yet, he began his memoir by stating he blamed his parents' divorce and the subsequent trauma on his father Kirk's many affairs.
It turned out to be a case of like father, like son, for Michael, who became known for his many dates.
He recalled meeting Lee Purcell on the set of their 1970 movie, Adam at 6 A.M. Michael was single and Lee was married, but they ended up having a 'passionate affair' while filming
Michael got to work on Summertree, where he met and fell in love with Brenda Vaccaro. Yet Michael's work kept him away for long periods, and Brenda began an affair with fellow actor Don Stroud (Michael and Brenda pictured in 1976)
While working on 1971's Summertree he fell in love with co-star Brenda Vaccaro.

articles.title_zh: Pentagon unveils US$350 million quantum computing push as China rivalry grows
articles.content_orig:
New initiative aims to strengthen US military capabilities as Washington and Beijing compete for leadership in advanced technology
The Pentagon announced on Thursday a new multimillion-dollar initiative for “maintaining American leadership” in quantum computing capabilities amid accelerating competition between the US and China over the military application of advanced technology.
In a press release, the Office of the Under Secretary of Defence for Research and Engineering, which serves as the US Department of Defence’s chief technology adviser, announced that the new initiative, worth around US$350 million, is aimed at strengthening US leadership in quantum computing capabilities to “support national security”.
Quantum computing dominance is a “critical priority” for the Trump administration, said Emil Michael, undersecretary of defence for research and engineering, citing a June executive order to accelerate the technology’s deployment, commercialisation and domestic manufacturing across the US.
“Maintaining American leadership in this field is essential to preserving our technological edge,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Thousands of Spaniards march to mark death of octogenarian at heart of housing protests
articles.title_zh: Thousands of Spaniards march to mark death of octogenarian at heart of housing protests
articles.content_orig:
Rally to remember woman, 87, whose rent battle with investment firm triggered nationwide protests over housing crisis
About 20,000 people took part in a march through the centre of Madrid on Thursday evening in memory of María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her flat in the capital a fortnight before her death triggered mass protests over Spain’s housing crisis .
The pensioner, whose flat had been bought by an investment firm that sought to increase her rent by 230%, had become the public face of the crisis before her death in hospital on Wednesday night.
Abascal’s eviction unleashed waves of demonstrations across Spain, led to the setting up of a protest camp in the centre of the capital, and prompted the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to try to make the rental market more equitable. When those measures were voted down by rightwing and far-right parties last week, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, announced a snap general election , to be held on 29 November.
Anger over the plight of the woman who had become known around the country as Maricarmen remained undimmed a few hours after her death. On the pavement across from the apartment building where she had lived for seven decades, a steady stream of people visited a small, steadily growing memorial. Some came to light candles or leave flowers, while others left handwritten messages such as, “You made history Maricarmen,” and “Thank you for changing Spain”. Sara, 41, who had come with her young son and a sign that read, “Maricarmen, we’ll fight for you”, said: “We’re here because I think Maricarmen’s death shows how institutions can kill a person by failing to care for them.”
For many, the site was a reminder of all that Maricarmen had gone through as she tried to stay in her home, fending off three eviction attempts before the investment firm succeeded in forcing her out. “When people are protected less than investors, that leads to these kinds of things happening,” Sara added. “This woman could have died – if she had died of natural causes – she could have died peacefully in her home.”
Jaime, 34, pointed to all that Maricarmen had come to represent, particularly in a country like Spain, where social rights are supposedly guaranteed. “She had become a symbol, albeit one she never wanted to be, of the fight for decent housing,” he said. “So I came here because I think it’s important to restore some of the respect that Spanish society took away from Maricarmen.”
Visitors included some of the housing campaigners who had helped Maricarmen fight off previous eviction attempts. “This is really hard to take,” said Miguel, 59, fighting back tears as he added a red rose to the memorial. “When money is more powerful than people’s lives, it’s unbelievable.”
He said he hoped Maricarmen’s death would mark a turning point in Spain. “At least now we’re talking about this and putting names to those who are being evicted,” he said. “Because until now, there were 44 people a day being forced out of their homes. To the people in power, those are just numbers – now at least we’ve started putting names to those going through this.”
The Madrid tenants’ union announced a commemorative march at 8pm on Wednesday from the camp in the Puerta del Sol square to Abascal’s flat.
“Farewell, Maricarmen!” the union said in a post on social media . “Tonight we’ll honour you with a march … to the place that was your home for 70 years, and where you just wanted to stay until the end.”
Abascal’s ordeal has made housing a key issue in the forthcoming election, with Sánchez’s government seeking to push a redrafted package of measures through the council that operates when parliament has been dissolved. Meanwhile, the rightwing and far-right parties that opposed the legislation in congress last week have accused the prime minister of failing to act to address the housing crisis over the course of his eight years in office.
Sánchez offered his condolences to Abascal’s family and friends on Wednesday night. “A hug also to everyone who’s feeling this loss today as their own,” he wrote on social media. “Rest in peace.”
after newsletter promotion
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party (PP), which voted against last week’s emergency measures, also offered his condolences.
“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he wrote on social media. “When a person dies, there should be nothing but respect.”
The following day, however, Feijóo accused the government of trying to “manipulate the emotions of the Spanish people” by focusing on one particular eviction when there had been countless others during Sánchez’s time in office.
PP politicians also joined forces with the far right on Thursday to veto attempts to hold a minute’s silence for Maricarmen in Madrid’s regional parliament and the country’s senate. In Madrid’s municipal council, meanwhile, a rightwing attempt to block a minute’s silence was thwarted by opposition parties.
Abascal’s death has prompted reflection on how she had been treated by politicians and the media. The far-right Vox party, which also voted down the new decrees, had falsely suggested that Maricarmen would have had a home had she been an immigrant from North Africa , while one commentator had opined that “Maricarmen was chosen during a casting call for people facing eviction” to become a leftwing saint.
At least two far-right figures, including one of Vox’s MEPs, sought to sow doubt over the cause of Abascal’s death, with one even suggesting an autopsy should be carried out to determine whether the government had been involved . Another wrote : “Maricarmen was probably already made to send in her postal vote before they did her in. I expect anything from this scum.”

The US government ⁠is suspending Microsoft, Adobe and ⁠several large IT firms from a programme that allows skilled foreign workers to gain permanent residency, senior US officials have announced, citing alleged fraud, and as part ‌of an effort to push companies to hire more Americans.
“Our message to Microsoft is: you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” US Vice-President J.D. Vance said on Thursday.
Vance said the programme required companies to advertise jobs in the US before applying to the Department of Labour to show they needed to give a foreign worker a green card because of a lack of American staff.
“They’ll put an advertisement in a small-town newspaper. They’ll go out there and say that ‘We have advertised for a position with our company, and nobody is responding to it,’” Vance said.

articles.title_orig: Chinese military facility in Laos raises questions about Beijing’s Indo-Pacific reach - VOA
articles.title_zh: Chinese military facility in Laos raises questions about Beijing’s Indo-Pacific reach - VOA
articles.content_orig:
New ‘support and training centre’ prompts concern in region but China says it is ‘not directed at any third party’
Satellite images show attack jets stationed at a new Chinese military facility in Laos , which opened last week and gives Beijing’s air force its first foothold in mainland south-east Asia.
Images provided by the commercial satellite provider Vantor show eight light attack aircraft positioned at Ban Keun airport alongside what appear to be more than a dozen military vehicles lined up in rows.
The planes’ shape matches that of the Chinese-made Hongdu JL-8 jet, a two-seat trainer that can be deployed in combat to carry bombs. Laos is reported to have four such aircraft, according to the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.
In a rare example of Beijing’s overseas military expansion, China opened what it said was a joint “support and training centre” at Ban Keun on 29 September.
The airport, about ⁠30 miles (50km) north of Vientiane, the capital of Laos, has been significantly expanded over the past year. Satellite images taken months ago show farmland and dirt paths where there are now new buildings and a paved runway.
Aside from its island bases in the South China Sea, Beijing does not have a significant network of military outposts in other countries, and the Laos airbase would be its first facility in another country capable of handling fighter jets.
The new satellite images, taken a day after the announcement and first reported by Reuters, show extensive construction work that appears to be focused on a future runway extension, which could make the airport capable of handling larger planes such as bombers.
In its announcement last week, China’s defence ministry said the new centre would “help Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots” and was not “directed against any third party”.
Governments will be watching closely for signs of deployments or the installation of defence equipment that may serve wider military ambitions. After the announcement, the Singapore-based security analyst Collin Koh said it “may not be wrong to conclude this is the first full-fledged PLA [People’s Liberation Army] overseas base in south-east Asia”.
Over the past two decades, China has built up an extensive network of outposts on islands in the disputed South China Sea, including airbases with air defence installations. Otherwise, its navy’s sole overseas military base is a logistics base in Djibouti, on the coast of the Horn of Africa .
The Laos agreement follows a similar programme established in Cambodia, at the Ream naval base on the Gulf of Thailand, although that facility has no runway.
After years of speculation and denials , China announced in April last year that it had created the “joint logistics and training” facility in Cambodia. It said the centre would support the two militaries in “conducting regional counter-terrorism, disaster prevention and mitigation, humanitarian assistance, joint training and other operations”.
US forces are believed to have used Ban Keun airport in Laos during covert military operations at the height of the Vietnam war in the 1960s and 1970s. Its development will be monitored by Vietnam, which maintains disputes with China over the South China Sea, and Thailand, which shares a border with Laos.
After the announcement last week, Thailand’s defence ministry spokesperson said Bangkok considered itself a close partner of both Laos and China and saw it as Vientiane’s sovereign right to decide whether to grant permission for a Chinese base.
“Nevertheless, Thailand will continue to closely monitor developments and how the matter proceeds, particularly with regard to building mutual trust,” said R Adm Surasant Kongsiri.
China’s government did not mention sending aircraft to Laos in its initial announcement, while the government of Laos has not commented on the project.
The US-based Institute for the Study of War has described the Laos base as the “first PLA overseas military facility focused on air power”. In its assessment, the thinktank said the base was “not yet equipped to provide the PLA with the ability to execute major combat operations, unlike US military bases”.
It said the base would give the Chinese military alternate routes to access to the South China Sea and strategic air routes.
Reuters contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Columbus changed the world
articles.title_zh: Columbus changed the world
articles.content_orig:
An official website of the United States government
Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.
Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock A locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.
Columbus changed the world
His journey to the Americas began an era of exchange
Christopher Columbus, depicted in a 1904 chromolithograph, led the Niña, the Pinta and the Santa Maria across the Atlantic to the Americas in 1492. (© GraphicaArtis/Getty Images)
Christopher Columbus was not the first European to reach the Americas, a feat achieved by the Vikings. What’s more, Columbus died thinking he’d arrived in known lands in Asia rather than on a different continent.
Despite misunderstanding his location, Columbus would leave a legacy arguably more important than any explorer of his time.
The Italian navigator, sailing under the flag of Spain, landed on that first voyage in what is now the Bahamas on October 12, 1492. That journey led him to greatness, as subsequent voyages by Columbus and others would develop the Western Hemisphere and connect the Eastern and Western Hemispheres in important ways.
Columbus’ 1492 voyage across the Atlantic was “one of the most important moments in world history,” says Bradley Birzer, a history professor at Hillsdale College. It began a period when the Spanish would found settlements in the Caribbean and the Portuguese would claim Brazil.
His voyages inspired others to follow, including the Italian Amerigo Vespucci, after whom “the Americas” are named.
Colonies established subsequently by European powers formed the basis of modern-day Latin America. And English settlers who arrived in North America in the early 1600s sowed the seeds of the society that would become the United States on July 4, 1776.
“We’re not here if Columbus didn’t do what he did,” says Mike Gonzalez, a senior fellow at the Heritage Foundation, a Washington research organization.
Columbus’ explorations set the stage for what the late historian Alfred Crosby (1931–2018) calls the “Columbian exchange,” an interchange of plants and animals between the hemispheres. Crosby described the exchange as “spectacular and significant” for its effect on the future of agricultural activities and the growth and development of the modern Americas, Europe and Africa.
For example, corn, a crop native to the Americas, improved the diet of many Europeans — it was more drought-resistant and easier to grow than other vegetables. In Africa, cultivation of corn, which stores longer than other foods, facilitated the growth of states and commercial ties among various groups, according to the Encyclopedia Britannica .
Other native American crops, such as potatoes and tomatoes, became widespread in Europe and staples in Ireland and Italy, respectively.
Demand for American tobacco by Europeans provided an economic boon to the British colonies. Chocolate (made from cacao) and hot peppers from Central and South America also found their way to the Old World, a direct result of Columbus’ voyages.
On the other side of the exchange, Columbus brought horses to the Americas. The animals revolutionized life for native cultures as hunters found that riding to hunt bison was effective.
Cattle and sheep brought from Europe also became important sources of food, clothing and shelter for American tribes. As U.S. pioneers moved westward during the 19th century, cattle pulled them in covered wagons.
“All of these things just transformed North and South America,” Birzer says.

articles.title_orig: Grandmother of 12 holds plank for 5 hours in new world record attempt - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Grandmother of 12 holds plank for 5 hours in new world record attempt - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
A grandmother of 12 is being credited for breaking her own Guinness World Record for a woman holding a plank move for the longest time period.
DonnaJean Wilde made her potential record-breaking attempt at the Huntsman World Senior Games in Utah this week and completed a plank hold for five hours.
Guinness World Records confirmed to ABC News that Wilde's title record, which she achieved on March 21, 2024, is 4 hours, 30 minutes and 11 seconds. The organization said it has received an application for Wilde's newest record attempt and will review evidence before declaring a new record.
"I always wondered if I could have gone to five [hours]," Wilde told ABC News' Danny New of her motivation to break her own plank hold record.
According to World Senior Games, the record attempt began at 3:03 p.m. MT, with judges rotating out every hour until 8:03 p.m. MT, when WIlde's attempt ended.
"Some of them would come right down to me: 'Go, DonnaJean, go! You're doing great!'" Wilde said of the judges.
The 61-year-old -- who lives in Alberta, Canada -- said her training to prepare for her record attempt included having her 3-year-old granddaughter, Rose, lie on her back while she planked.
Wilde said she wasn't certain she would be able to accomplish her five-hour feat and even considered giving up during the attempt.
"I told [my husband] Randy, 'I'm done. I'm going down.' And they [the audience] all chanted me to the end. They got me through the last 10 minutes," Wilde said.
If her latest record attempt is recognized, Wilde would have earned her third Guinness title, following her previous plank record and her other record for the most pushups done in an hour by a woman, at 1,575.
It's another impressive feat for Wilde, who said she didn't rest for long after her latest plank feat. The morning after her record attempt, she ran in a 3,000-meter race.
As for her next record attempt, Wilde said she hopes to do at least 1,600 pushups in an hour and break her second record title.

articles.title_orig: ‘We don’t want this right now’: James Talarico off the trail with the flu
articles.title_zh: ‘We don’t want this right now’: James Talarico off the trail with the flu
articles.content_orig:
The bitter fight over a Texas Senate seat that Democrats believe is within reach for the first time in decades should be ramping up right now.
But in the final push, when campaigns believe most voters are finally tuning in, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has been off the trail for in-person events in the state for 12 days.
His campaign says he is suffering from the flu and expected to be back in action this weekend.
While he has appeared virtually at a forum, Talarico’s last in-person event in the state was on Sept. 26. He visited New York on Sept. 29 for a private fundraiser and, according to the virtual remarks he gave to the Hispanic Business Council the following day, he returned to Dallas and visited urgent care.
It has all prompted a stream of fodder from his opponent, Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose campaign is calling on Talarico to produce a photo of himself with a newspaper showing today’s date.
“We have a simple request: proof of life,” Paxton campaign spokeswoman Madison Cercy said. “James Talarico wants to represent 31 million Texans in the U.S. Senate, but for 12 days, he’s hidden from every one of them. There’s a reason they call it ‘Texas Tough,’ and it’s not because Texans hide at the first sign of trouble. If James Talarico is too fragile to face Texans, he has no business asking for their vote.”
While some Texas Democrats are shrugging it off, it is causing some consternation.
“He’s like, really sick. Believe me, we don’t want this right now,” a Texas Democrat involved in the Talarico race said. “We’d rather have him on the trail.”
Talarico’s absence is undoubtedly a curveball for Democrats who believe his best asset is connecting with potential voters in person. It also presents a turnaround for Talarico, who had been visible in the early days of the campaign as Paxton was off the trail.
“After holding more than 100 public events and shaking tens of thousands of hands, James came down with the flu but will be back on the trail this weekend,” Talarico spokesman JT Ennis said in a statement. “Ken Paxton has been ignoring Texans this entire campaign, and his priorities are clear: he doesn’t answer to the people of this state — he answers to his billionaire megadonors and special interests.”
Democratic political strategist Ed Espinoza said that some supporters he’s spoken to noted his absence from in-person campaign events and lamented that they wanted to make sure other people were seeing enough of him.
Espinoza, though, said he didn’t think that would be a problem.
“Look, he’s got like $80 million of ads going right now. So I think that’s pretty good scale for him at the moment,” Espinoza said. “He may be recovering at home, but he is still everywhere.”
Espinoza said that he’d rather Talarico be off the trail and recovering now rather than be hampered even closer to the election.
Texas Democratic Party Chair Kendall Scudder said Paxton “caught a little bit of a break” with Talarico’s absence.
“It’s certainly not ideal, but we want to make sure he does everything he needs to to make sure that he’s healthy and ready to go. We’re in the homestretch, and it sounds like he’s on the mend, and that’s great news,” Scudder said. “He’s a phenomenal candidate, he’s been working really hard for a long time, and everyone gets sick every now and then.”
To Talarico’s great fortune, distractions have abounded. A steady flow of damaging audio featuring Paxton saying that Trump’s midterm convention wasn’t helpful or that cuts to “mandatory spending” were inevitable has grabbed public attention.
At the same time, both Paxton and Trump have hit Talarico for being off the trail.
“You haven’t seen him in a couple of weeks,” Trump said at a Wednesday rally in San Antonio. “I hear the guy has disappeared. Nobody knows. You know where he is? He’s sick, because he’s forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.”
After the rally, Trump posted on social media a demand that Talarico show up in person to debate Paxton.
“He should immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able, one of the best Attorney Generals in the Country, and will soon be, hopefully, a United States Senator representing the Great People of Texas!” Trump said in a Truth Social post .
It was a twist, given that Talarico has repeatedly called on Paxton to debate. Though not on the trail yet, Talarico did respond over social media:
“President Trump just said Ken Paxton should debate,” Talarico wrote. “I agree. Ball’s in your court @KenPaxtonTX .”
Natasha Korecki is a senior national political reporter for NBC News.
Ryan Chandler is a correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Military ordered to be ready for possible Iran strikes as Trump weighs timing
articles.title_zh: Military ordered to be ready for possible Iran strikes as Trump weighs timing
articles.content_orig:
After having faced fierce backlash, President Donald Trump on Wednesday sought to clean up incendiary comments he made earlier this week, when he said Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego.
Trump’s original remarks , made at a campaign rally in Nebraska, seemed to refer to what would happen if Iran had a nuclear weapon.
“They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego,” Trump said Monday to cheers from the crowd.
He recast those remarks Wednesday night at a rally in San Antonio as he tried to explain the Iran war, saying he had “no choice” if the U.S. were to keep Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.
“You want to see problems? And I said it the other day: Let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. Let them hit. You want to see a horror show? You want to see problems?”
“Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles if you want to see some bad things happen. You want to see a country that would be in free fall?”
This time, however, he added: “We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities. We protect our country. We’re not letting that happen.”
Trump’s initial remarks sparked backlash, particularly from California Democrats. Gov. Gavin Newsom accused Trump of prodding foreign enemies to take out U.S. cities. “He is deranged and dangerous,” Newsom wrote on social media.
“To do that makes us look ridiculous on the world stage, but it also gives a green light to Iran, the nation that he chose to attack, the green light to attack our cities,” Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass told NBC News after Wednesday’s rally.
Bass said she may call on Congress to investigate Trump’s comments.
Trump’s comments Wednesday came in a winding speech at a boisterous rally that stretched for about an hour and 45 minutes, with numerous interruptions from protesters. At one point, a protester who had been heckling Trump was grabbed by a person in the audience in an incident captured on video. A man in the crowd, wearing what looked to be a red “Make America Great Again” hat, grabbed the protester by the hair. Others in the crowd tried to free the protester.
The evening was meant to boost Texas Republicans, including Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running for the Senate in a pitched battle against Democrat James Talarico. In a reflection of Trump’s low favorability ratings, even in the red state of Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott — a staunch Trump ally — said he could not attend because of a scheduling conflict.
Capping the night, Trump announced that he would award former Major League Baseball pitcher and seven-time Cy Young Award winner Rogers Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
“We’re giving him the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and along with the Congressional Medal of Honor, it’s the highest award bestowed upon anyone,” Trump said, adding he would help him get into the Baseball Hall of Fame someday. “He deserves it.”
Clemens, a Texan, was accused of using performance-enhancing drugs late in his baseball career. He maintains he has never used PEDs.
On Wednesday night, Clemens took the stage at Trump’s invitation, saying he was “stunned.”
“This supersedes anything that obviously I’ve done in my playing career,” Clemens said. “To get it from this man, this president, there wouldn’t be another president I’d want to get it from.”
Natasha Korecki is a senior national political reporter for NBC News.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.
Bill Feather is an assignment editor for NBC Los Angeles who covers general assignment and daily breaking news, primarily in Southern California.

articles.title_orig: The Trump administration is suspending Microsoft from a green card program, alleging fraud
articles.title_zh: The Trump administration is suspending Microsoft from a green card program, alleging fraud
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Department of Labor announced it would suspend Microsoft and Adobe from its Permanent Labor Certification program on Thursday, Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said, as the Trump administration continues to take aim at immigration and foreign hiring programs ahead of November's midterm elections.
Sonderling said the Labor Department won't accept or process any new applications under the program for a host of companies, including Cognizant, Infosys, Capgemini, Tata, Wipro and HCL.
The secretary said Adobe and Microsoft were also suspended "due to multiple active federal investigations."
"Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost 3 million foreign workers. They've received over 230,000 H-1B visas approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications. That's hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers," Sonderling said.
Vice President JD Vance criticized Microsoft specifically, pointing to the firm's 6,000 layoffs in 2025. Vance claimed that the company "replaced" those workers with people on H-1B visas.
"So we're going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we're also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first," Vance said.
Microsoft responded to Vance's claims and defended its hiring practices in a statement Thursday, saying "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans."
"Of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees," the company said.
President Donald Trump is set to award the National Medal of Science to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and other leading technology CEOs on Thursday at the same summit where the suspension announcement was made.
Nadella is from India and moved to the U.S. in 1988. He joined Microsoft in 1992.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su are also being honored at Thursday's medal ceremony. Each of the leaders immigrated to the U.S. Musk was born in South Africa and Su and Huang were born in Taiwan.
"It's one thing if you want to bring in a person like Elon Musk," Vance said. "I think 99% of American citizens look at somebody like Elon Musk or Lisa Su, the CEO of AMD, and they say, obviously, if that person wants to come in and build something great in the United States of America, we support that."
Tech giants like Microsoft, Google , Amazon and Apple have been among the top sponsors of H-1B visas for decades. This year, Amazon had the highest number of petitions at 35,426 workers, followed by Cognizant and EY, according to 2026 data from Levels.fyi .
Microsoft was a close fourth at 21,706 petitions for 2026, with a median base salary of $180,710.
Microsoft said that petitions were only filed for workers "who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," and said Microsoft's wages for H-1B workers were among the highest of all H-1B filings.
CNBC has reached out to Adobe for comment.

articles.title_orig: Trump says anyone who does not refer to AI as ‘super intelligence’ is ‘THE ENEMY'
articles.title_zh: Trump says anyone who does not refer to AI as ‘super intelligence’ is ‘THE ENEMY'
articles.content_orig:
New alliances between the White House, the Pentagon, US intelligence and AI companies are looming ominously
Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, writing to you as I sit under yellowing leaves in New York. Today in tech, we’re discussing technocracy.
Donald Trump made a series of moves over the past week that make it clear his power is becoming synonymous with artificial intelligence.
The new tight alliances between the White House, the Pentagon, US intelligence agencies and AI companies loom ominously over governments and companies, particularly in Europe, that rely on American AI.
Last Tuesday, Trump and six AI CEOs signed what he called a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. The vague agreement stipulates a framework for what Trump called “tremendous self-policing”, reiterating his point that AI companies can act as their own watchmen. Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg , Jensen Huang and Dario Amodei signed.
Zuckerberg hand-guided the writing of that agreement, Semafor reported. The pact reportedly arose from a conversation between the Meta CEO and House speaker, Mike Johnson, at the US state dinner for Xi Jinping, which preceded the conclave of the tech CEOs. Zuckerberg circulated a draft of the agreement in advance of the convening, and Huang threw his support behind it, per Semafor.
It is one thing for tech executives to dine at the White House to curry favor with the president; it is entirely another to have them draft the terms of executive orders. Silicon Valley’s CEOs are writing contracts that bear the White House letterhead, entrenching their interests and their power.
“It’s almost like a constitution in a way, and the biggest ​people in the world signed that, and ​I signed it as president, and it really ⁠is a form of protection,” Trump said. Famously, constitutions are legally binding, which Zuckerberg and Trump’s agreement is not.
The president also decreed that government documents render any reference to “artificial intelligence” as “super intelligence”. How loyal will they be to his rebrand?
At least one acquiesced immediately: Musk copied the renaming by changing the name of one of his company’s subsidiaries from SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. The change coincided with the multi-CEO’s re-entry into government work more than a year after his explosive term at Doge ended. On Thursday, the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth , named Musk to a taskforce to study the future of warfare alongside Palmer Luckey and Emil Michael, dubbed Project Meridian. The trio of men will release a report in 120 days with public recommendations on how to achieve “absolute technological dominance on the next-generation battlefield”, in the words of Hegseth.
Over the weekend, the president announced that he had appointed Jay Clayton, director of national intelligence, as the AI czar of his administration.
Trump’s first AI czar was a Silicon Valley insider. David Sacks is a venture capitalist who championed growth and deregulation during his term as a special government employee. He maintained direct financial stakes in multiple AI companies while working with the White House, indicating his ultimate goal was to build a bigger fortune. (He’s made a name for himself recently championing AI accelerationism, the opposing philosophical camp to the “doomerism” of the Anthropic employees who prophesy extinction.)
Read more: ‘An out-of-touch Silicon Valley radical’: meet Trump’s AI whisperer pushing for limited regulation
The second czar, Clayton, is the leader of the US’s spy agencies, a job he will continue to hold in addition to overseeing AI initiatives. His joint appointment sends a very different message, one echoed by Hegseth: AI will supercharge the offensive capabilities of the US government, in particular surveillance and the gathering of intel. Clayton’s ascendancy has major worldwide implications: US spying agencies dictating global AI policy does not bode well for the sovereignty of other nations that need cutting-edge AI.
after newsletter promotion
The US economy is already extremely dependent on the growth of the artificial intelligence sector. The companies whose leaders attended Trump’s summit are responsible for the majority of the US stock market’s growth over the past five years.
The latest moves by Trump’s administration signal that American power is likewise inextricable from AI, synonymous: executive authority, military might and the government’s information. The White House pledge binds Trump and the AI CEOs together; Hegseth’s taskforce ties the Pentagon to Musk and Luckey’s visions of automated war in space; and making Clayton the AI czar predicts an era of AI-enabled spying, of government knowledge being gathered and filtered through large language models.
One point of striking divergence: labor. The economy writ large may rest on AI, but the workers of the US do not. The majority of the hiring happening in the US is not a result of AI companies’ growth, according to the US jobs report released on Friday. Far more people are being hired to work in healthcare, a sector that still needs human labor more than automated work. AI may fuel gross domestic product growth, but it is not driving job creation on a national scale.
