articles.title_orig: More physical activity may mean slower Parkinson’s disease progression
articles.title_zh: More physical activity may mean slower Parkinson’s disease progression
articles.content_orig:
Higher levels of physical activity were associated with slower cognitive decline and motor progression in mild-to-moderate Parkinson's disease (PD) over up to 7 years of follow-up, a longitudinal cohort study showed.
While the greatest cognitive benefits were observed in patients who reported more than 8 hours of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity per week, those who were active for at least 4 hours a week also showed slower decline than individuals who were less active. The same held true for motor progression, with all levels of activity showing some benefit but those getting more exercise reporting the slowest motor decline.
In additional analyses, vigorous activity showed no association with either outcome beyond that of total activity time. Recent activity remained associated with both outcomes after adjustment for activity in the 10 years before enrollment.
The data add to limited evidence on the relationship between physical activity and cognitive decline in PD and offer a longer-term picture of protective motor benefits that that short-duration trials were could not provide.
"Our findings suggest that physical activity may influence the cognitive trajectory of Parkinson's disease, alongside its motor benefits," senior investigator Alberto J. Espay, MD, MSc, a movement disorders specialist and professor of neurology at the University of Cincinnati, told Medscape Medical News .
"That is encouraging, but it does not establish that exercise prevents cognitive decline or dementia," Espay said, adding that randomized evidence is still needed, along with confirmation that the differences translate into preserved everyday function.
The study was published online October 7 in Neurology .
No drug has been proven to modify the course of PD. Exercise has been studied as one possible way to do so, and two randomized trials have shown short-term motor benefits.
In Park-in-Shape , 130 patients with early PD who completed 6 months of home-based aerobic exercise had a smaller increase in off-medication motor scores than an active control group.
In the phase 2 SPARX trial , 6 months of high-intensity treadmill exercise was associated with less motor worsening than usual care, whereas moderate-intensity exercise did not differ from usual care.
As reported previously by Medscape Medical News , a 2022 study in Neurology linked regular moderate-to-vigorous exercise in early PD with slower decline in processing speed.
But testing long-term effects in randomized trials is difficult because restricting physical activity in a control group for years is neither ethical nor practical, the investigators of the 2022 study wrote. Adherence problems and crossover between groups can also erode the difference in exposure over time.
To address the lack of long-term data, the current study's investigators analyzed data from 294 patients with mild-to-moderate PD (mean age, 66.4 years; 33% women) enrolled in the Cincinnati Cohort Biomarker Program between January 2019 and February 2025.
Clinical research fellows gave patients a structured interview, adapted from a questionnaire used in other large PD cohorts, that recorded weekly hours of moderate and vigorous activity at work, at home, and during recreation.
Moderate activities included brisk walking, nonstrenuous bicycling, doubles tennis, light swimming, and household chores. Vigorous activity included such activities as jogging, fast bicycling, aerobics, or snow shoveling.
Patients were divided into tertiles of total weekly activity: up to 4 hours, 4-8 hours, and more than 8 hours. Baseline Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and motor scores did not differ significantly across groups, although the most active patients were younger. Patients were followed for cognitive function for up to 5 years and up to 7 years for motor function (median follow-up for both, 3 years).
Motor scores were assessed while patients were in the "on" state, when their usual PD medication was taking effect.
In models adjusted for age, sex, disease duration, education, BMI, and baseline disease stage, each additional weekly hour of activity was associated with 0.035 fewer points in MoCA decline per year ( P < .001) and 0.082 fewer points in motor worsening per year ( P = .020).
The middle tertile also declined more slowly on the MoCA than the least active group ( P = .005), with no significant differences between the middle and highest tertile groups.
The cognitive association held after investigators excluded four participants in the least active group who declined unusually fast, whereas the motor association weakened.
On the motor examination section of the Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS-III), where higher scores indicate worse function, the average score at baseline was 23. Scores rose by 0.143 points per year in the least active group but fell by 0.783 points per year in the most active group.
The highest activity group reported significantly slower MDS-UPDRS-III progression than those who were physically active for fewer than 4 hours a week ( P = .048).
"Taken together, these results suggest that physical activity may provide dual clinical benefits by independently reducing both motor progression and cognitive decline in PD," researchers wrote. "Furthermore, the observed effects of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity were more strongly related to activity duration than intensity and were not explained by baseline activity level."
Study limitations include the observational design, self-reported activity, and a single-center cohort that was 98.3% White. Patients excluded from the analysis, most often for missing activity data, were older and had higher baseline motor scores than those included.
While previous studies have demonstrated the potential short-term neuroprotective benefits of exercise, researchers say the new findings fill a gap in the literature on long-term effects. But the question of how physical activity is linked to cognitive and motor function preservation remains unanswered.
"I suspect several pathways work together, rather than one mechanism explaining both findings," Espay said. "Improved blood flow, reduced inflammation, and greater capacity for synaptic adaptation could support the brain networks involved in both movement and cognition."
The range of biological effects is what makes exercise a compelling candidate for disease modification, said Bastiaan R. Bloem, MD, PhD, professor of neurology and director of the Center of Expertise for Parkinson and Movement Disorders at Radboud University Medical Center, Nijmegen, Netherlands. Bloem led the Park-in-Shape trial but was not involved in the new study.
"It has anti-inflammatory components. It enhances blood flow. It increases neurotrophic factors. It drives neuroplasticity," he said.
Bloem's group found in a follow-up imaging analysis of Park-in-Shape that patients who exercised built new functional connectivity in the brain and had less brain atrophy than a stretching control group. The new study's greatest strength is its long follow-up, since randomized trials have often been limited to months, he said.
But Espay said that whether those biological pathways explain the associations seen in the Cincinnati cohort is not yet clear.
"We cannot establish the direction of causation from these data, and the relationship may run both ways," he said, adding that people with slower progression may be better able to stay active. Only a clinical trial can settle the question, he added.
The investigators wrote that examining the relationship between physical activity and disease-related biomarkers — including alpha-synuclein, amyloid-beta, and tau in cerebrospinal fluid — could help clarify whether the benefits are disease-specific. That analysis is planned but has not yet begun, Espay said.
Daniel M. Corcos, PhD, studies exercise in PD in the Department of Physical Therapy and Human Movement Sciences at Northwestern University,

articles.title_orig: A year into Trump’s peace plan, Netanyahu stands in the way of rebuilding
articles.title_zh: A year into Trump’s peace plan, Netanyahu stands in the way of rebuilding
articles.content_orig:
Three years after Hamas militants launched their assault on southern Israel, killing 1,200 people, taking 251 others hostage and triggering Israel's war in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians, CBS News met two teenagers on both sides of the Gaza border to find out how they are coping.
Ron Shargian, 15, said growing up in southern Israel has meant learning to live with fear. He was 12 when he watched Hamas militants on paragliders soar over a wall meant to protect his community.
"It feels like some kind of nightmare," he told CBS News three years later, calling the experience on that fateful day surreal, "and something I wouldn't believe if anyone told me it's going to happen."
The attackers killed 17 of his neighbors in Netiv HaAsara, the Israeli community that was closest to the Gaza border.
As the assault unfolded, he and his family locked themselves inside their home's bomb shelter.
"Every time the gunshots get close to you, you think that that's the end, that they're coming to your house now," he recalled.
His family escaped after 11 hours, when security forces came to the rescue, but like thousands of other Israelis displaced by the war, they couldn't go back home, at least not right away.
After Oct. 7, Shargian's family lived in a hotel for evacuees, and then in Tel Aviv, and then in another hotel, and then a year and a half in the coastal town of Gan Yavne. Finally, a little over a year ago, his family returned to their home.
"It was really hard to come back," he said. "But I also anticipated it very much. I really missed my home, my friends, the community — it's something that you don't have anywhere else."
Across the border in Gaza, safe places have been hard for Palestinian children to find since Israel launched its full-scale military assault in retaliation for the Hamas attack.
"Lots of things has been destroyed for me," Kazem Doghmash told CBS News. He was 11 when the war started.
Israel pummeled Gaza for years with daily airstrikes in a grueling war that, despite a cease-fire in place since last October ending major combat, continues to claim lives three years later . Palestinian officials in Gaza say more than 1,400 people have been killed in Gaza since the cease-fire officially came into effect.
"They say a lot of times that the war will finish, but the war has been not finished, the war has been more difficult," said Doghmash, who is now 14.
"Before the war, I am just being a kid," he said, remembering it as "a good life."
In Israel, Shargian said he struggles with how to think about people on the other side of the Gaza border after everything that happened.
"I don't know if there are good people there," he said. "Up until October 7th, I thought that we could make peace. But from that day, something inside me broke."
He is trying to move forward and lead a normal teenage life — learning the guitar, hanging out with friends at the beach, and he told CBS News the wider conflict now engulfing the Middle East can, at times, even feel distant.
"I don't think we feel the war so much, like, it's in other countries," he said.
When the sound of a rocket or an air raid siren jolts him back to reality, he said like most Israelis, he takes it in his stride.
"Because we're so used to this reality," he said. "So, we just don't make a big deal out of it."
But even though it has happened throughout his life, he said he still feels it inside, every time he and his family or friends hear an alarm and have to rush for shelter.
"Your muscles get tight and you have an adrenaline rush," he said. "It's something we just got used to."
Moving forward has been hard for Doghmash, too. He still can't think about returning to normal teenage pursuits.
"My life has been destroyed," he said. "My school has been destroyed, a lot of things have been destroyed for me."
"We are focusing [on] how we're going to live," he said.
But he hasn't given up on his dreams. He told CBS News he hopes to become a doctor, and he has resumed studying at the British International School in Gaza —   in its new location, as the original building was destroyed by Israeli airstrikes —   where his favorite subject is English.
As he led CBS News through the rubble of what used to be his family's home, he longed for anything resembling a return to his life before the war.
"We need to live in a good life, not to just, thinking how we're gonna get food and the water," he said. "We're gonna need to go to school, to go, to be happy and smile."
The United Nations Children's Fund says more than 21,000 Palestinian children have been reported killed in Gaza since Oct. 7, 2023, as a result of Israel's counteroffensive.
Dozens of Israeli children have died, too, including 37 killed in the initial Hamas attacks.
Despite everything they've been through, both boys are still finding moments in life to just be kids.
CBS News' Becky Perlow and Anas Zeyad Fteiha contributed to this report.
Tucker  Reals contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Risk and strategy for Indonesia – China Marine Scientific Research cooperation
articles.title_zh: Risk and strategy for Indonesia – China Marine Scientific Research cooperation
articles.content_orig:
During the Indonesia-China foreign ministers’ meeting in Jakarta in August this year, both countries agreed to make maritime cooperation one of the main pillars of Indonesia-China strategic dialogue. One of the maritime cooperation priority agendas discussed was marine scientific research . But with China often using marine scientific research as part of its assertive maritime strategy , Indonesia should develop a plan to ensure that cooperation in this area will not threaten Indonesia’s security.
In the past few years, China has intensified marine scientific research. According to CSIS , China has more marine scientific research vessels operating in the Indo-Pacific than any other country, including the United States. Chinese research vessels operate in various locations from the South China Sea to the Indian Ocean . So how can Indonesia and China advance marine scientific research that benefits both countries while keeping national security interests in mind?
Indeed, the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) encourages cooperation on marine scientific research to advance human knowledge of the ocean. Given the vastness and depth of the world’s oceans, scientists often consider them largely unexplored. But it is important to note that under UNCLOS, marine scientific research should be conducted for peaceful purposes and should not become the basis for asserting maritime claims.
For Indonesia, the world’s largest archipelagic state with a vast maritime area within its exclusive economic zone and continental shelf, knowledge of what lies beneath its waters is critical. However, with limited technology and resource capacity, international cooperation on marine scientific research is becoming very important.
But despite the benefits that Indonesia may get by conducting marine scientific research cooperation with China, it also carry significant risks. In recent years, China’s research activities have operated illegally in Indonesian waters. For instance, the research vessel Haiyang Dizhi 10 has often conducted illegal surveys in Indonesia’s Exclusive Economic Zone. Moreover, Chinese-owned uncrewed underwater vehicles (UUVs) have also been found operating in Indonesian archipelagic waters.
With these growing concerns, Indonesia should consider three things when developing marine scientific research that can benefit both Indonesia and China.
First, marine scientific research cooperation needs a clear definition and scope. Under UNCLOS, there are no clear definitions of marine scientific research. As a result, different parties interpret for themselves what counts as marine scientific research. A wide range of generally recognized activities include seabed topography, geology, fisheries ecosystems, marine ecosystems, genetic resources, and environmental protection.
Some other activities, despite using some of the same capabilities and data collection methods, are usually not regarded as marine scientific research. For instance, surveillance for military purposes or survey activities for oil and gas exploration are often considered not part of academic marine scientific research.
When it comes to cooperation with China, however, this scope of research can be difficult to distinguish, particularly because of the strong link between Chinese research institutions and the People’s Liberation Army. Some reports suggest that Chinese university-based research institutions supply research to the PLA . Such a close relationship may expose Indonesia’s marine data and spatial information to Chinese military institutions.
Therefore, the cooperation agreement between Indonesia and China should clearly define what activities qualify as marine scientific research and how the data may be used.
Secondly, all cooperation projects should comply with UNCLOS jurisdictional regulations. For instance, marine scientific research in the EEZ, archipelagic waters, and territorial waters should be based on the consent of coastal states. Under UNCLOS, this consent has to be specific to each research project. Indonesia therefore should maintain the requirement to secure its consent for each research activity conducted in its maritime areas under the cooperation agreement.
In the past five years alone, at least three Chinese UUVs were found in Indonesian archipelagic waters in Lombok and South Sulawesi, accidentally discovered by local Indonesian fishermen. Chinese research institutions allegedly operated these UUVs without consent and permission from the Indonesian authorities. Therefore, those UUVs operated in Indonesian waters illegally and cannot be considered legitimate.
Moreover, the type of scientific research conducted and where it is conducted can sometimes be contested. For instance, in research related to hydrography and military activities, coastal states and major maritime powers often disagree. The United States and the United Kingdom consider hydrography and military research to be allowed within the EEZ, and reject efforts by coastal states with more restrictive policies to regulate such research.
Marine scientific research can also be sensitive, particularly in a contested maritime area. For instance, even though Indonesia does not recognize any overlapping maritime claim with China, Indonesia’s EEZ overlaps with China’s illegal nine-dash line. Therefore, any research activity conducted in the overlapping area could also become very sensitive.
Thirdly, it is important to have a reciprocal agreement between Indonesian and Chinese research institutions. It should not only allow Chinese institutions to conduct research in Indonesian waters, but also allow Indonesian scholars and researchers to conduct research in Chinese waters and access information from that research.
This reciprocal agreement could not only give Indonesian research institutions more data and information, but it could also increase the possibility of technology transfer for Indonesian researchers and institutions.
Marine scientific research cooperation between Indonesia and China is important for both countries. However, given China’s aggressive maritime behavior, which often uses marine scientific research to assert its aggressive and illegal claims, Indonesia should ensure any such cooperation follows these principles so that it is not co-opted to serve China’s interests.
Cover photo: Cen Yunpeng/Xinhua/Getty Images
Aristyo Rizka Darmawan is an Assistant Professor of international law at Universitas Indonesia and a PhD Scholar at the Australian National University.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Isaias forecast to bring dangerous storm surge, with millions under warnings in US
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias forecast to bring dangerous storm surge, with millions under warnings in US
articles.content_orig:
Residents in areas from the mouth of the Mississippi River to Florida urged to ‘evacuate if told to do so’
Millions of people from Louisiana to Florida are under hurricane warnings on Thursday as Hurricane Isaias looked set to head towards the US Gulf coast with weather officials warning of dangerous storm surge, hurricane-force winds, heavy rainfall, and flooding.
Isaias intensified into a hurricane from a tropical storm on Wednesday night, becoming the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season.
In an advisory on Thursday morning, the National Weather Service (NWS) said that Isaias, which is currently a category 1 hurricane with sustained winds of 85mph with higher gusts, is expected to pass to the north of the Yucatán peninsula later on Thursday before reaching the northern Gulf coast where it is expected to make landfall late Friday or early Saturday.
The NWS said that Isaias is “expected to strengthen and be a strong hurricane when it approaches the northern Gulf Coast on Friday” and warned that a “life-threatening storm surge” is expected along a portion of the northern Gulf coast.
Storm surge warnings, which are issued when there is a “danger of life-threatening indundation from rising water moving inland from the coastline”, are in effect on Thursday from the mouth of the Mississippi River to Steinhatchee, Florida , and residents in the warning area have been urged to “follow advice given by local officials and evacuate if told to do so”.
Hurricane warnings, meaning that hurricane conditions are expected, are also in effect in the areas from Ocean Springs, Mississippi to the Bay/Gulf county line, Florida. The NWS has warned that “damaging hurricane force-winds are expected over portions of the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama, and southern Mississippi” and urged residents to prepare for the possibility of “long-duration power outages”.
The NWS warned on Thursday: “Gusty winds are possible in portions of the Yucatan Peninsula today.”
Isaias is also expected to bring “areas of heavy rainfall” to the central Gulf coast and much of the south-east from Friday into the weekend, and the NWS said that flash and urban flooding, along with isolated river flooding, will be possible. From Friday through the weekend, Isaias is expected to produce rainfall amounts of three to seven inches across the central US Gulf coast extending from far south-eastern Louisiana to the Florida Big Bend region.
“Localized totals up to 15 inches are possible, particularly within banding across the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend,” the NWS said.
Isolated tornadoes are also possible on Friday night in coastal areas of Alabama and the Florida Panhandle and far southwestern Georgia, the NWS said, adding that “the tornado threat will continue Saturday for eastern Alabama, Georgia and northern Florida.”
On Wednesday, the Alabama governor, Kay Ivey, declared a state of emergency in 40 counties, saying that the order “will allow us to take any needed steps ahead of landfall”. The emergency declaration is scheduled to remain in effect until 14 October.
The Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, also declared a state of emergency this week for 25 counties as the state prepares.
“This order ensures communities have the time and resources necessary to prepare for potential severe weather impacts to the Panhandle and Big Bend region of Florida,” DeSantis said in the announcement.
At the local level, officials in Okaloosa county, Florida, declared a local state of emergency on Wednesday and ordered some residents in coastal areas to evacuate. Panama City also declared a local state of emergency “due to the potential effects of Isaias and its near threat to the citizens and property in Panama City and surrounding communities”.
Several school districts in Alabama and Florida have also announced closures ahead of Isaias.
The Federal Aviation Administration also warned on Thursday that Isaias may “lead to Gulf route closures”.
In Tennessee, the NWS office in Morristown warned that “remnants of Hurricane Isaias will bring heavy rain and strong, gusty winds to our area this weekend.” The office said that “high winds could top 60–70+ mph in the eastern TN mountains and foothills, with isolated flash flooding possible in heavy rainfall areas.”

articles.title_orig: Health officials report 74 new measles cases in Pennsylvania - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Health officials report 74 new measles cases in Pennsylvania - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Five people have died in the state so far this year.
Pennsylvania is reporting 74 new measles cases since Monday, the state's health department said Wednesday.
A total of 1,078 cases have been reported in the state so far this year. At least 207 people have been hospitalized and five people have died, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) .
"Of the 74 cases added, more than 40 represent individuals who were sick more than two weeks ago and are no longer contagious, but their cases were only recently reported and subsequently confirmed, the DOH said. Wednesday's update "does not reflect a current surge in new infections."
Of the five people who died, two of the deaths were among unvaccinated adults: an 18-year-old and a 40-year-old. The other two deaths were among infants who were too young to have received the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine.
The fifth death occurred in an unvaccinated resident of Lancaster County, in southeastern Pennsylvania, but it is unclear how old the individual is. Lancaster County is the epicenter of the state's outbreak, with 401 cases confirmed so far.
One-third of cases are among those under 18 years old and fewer than 1% of cases are among those fully vaccinated with the MMR shot, according to DOH data.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective in preventing measles infection and two doses are 97% effective, the CDC says.
Infants aged 6 to 11 months living in or traveling to high-risk outbreak areas may receive an early third dose of the MMR vaccine.
CDC data, however shows vaccination rates have been lagging in recent years. During the 2025-26 school year, 92.4% of kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, according to data. This is lower than the 95.2% seen in the 2019-20 school year, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic.
"State health center staff have administered more than 5,700 MMR vaccinations at 198 pop-up vaccination clinics in the affected communities since the outbreak began in late April," DOH wrote in a press release on Wednesday.
"Dozens of additional vaccine clinics are scheduled for the upcoming weeks and months, based on community interest and need," the press release continued. "In pop-up clinics and at state health centers combined, Department nurses have administered nearly 9,000 MMR vaccine doses to residents across the Commonwealth in 2026."

articles.title_orig: Cyborg Politics 3.0: AI and the Algorithms of Unpeace
articles.title_zh: Cyborg Politics 3.0: AI and the Algorithms of Unpeace
articles.content_orig:
https://doi.org/10.60965/bq31-tt86
Today’s debate about the perils and promises of artificial superintelligence is at once terrifyingly existential and astonishingly narrow. It is framed as a good vs. evil binary over humanity’s future: superabundant Utopia or humanity’s extinction. No-one can put a number on the probability of any outcome because the titans of Silicon Valley are accelerating into the unknown.
In this essay, author Alex de Waal argues that this framing misses what has already happened. AI has changed how we think, as members of a social-political collective. AI has hacked the operating system of society and is defining the questions to be posed and limiting the range of allowable answers to those questions.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he is considering asking FBI to investigate the death of Nolan Wells
articles.title_zh: Trump says he is considering asking FBI to investigate the death of Nolan Wells
articles.content_orig:
Lawyers for Wells’s family have called for a federal investigation into 18-year-old’s disappearance and death
On Wednesday, Donald Trump said he was considering asking the FBI to investigate the death of Nolan Wells, a Black college freshman who was last seen alive on a 4 July boating trip with friends.
Wells, 18, went missing while on Horn Island, a barrier island off the coast of Mississippi . His body was found on the island two days later. Wells’s cause and manner of death are still undetermined.
His disappearance and subsequent death have become a flashpoint for racial animosity in the country, drawing national scrutiny. During the Jackson county investigation into the case, social media became rife with misinformation about Wells, his family and his friends.
Wells’s mother, Christine Wells-Wonsley, started searching for him, leading to a photo of Wells with three white friends on a boat going viral.
In the months between Wells’s body being found and a Jackson county grand jury declining to indict anyone in his case, many have suggested that the treatment Wells’s family has received by local officials would have been different if they were white.
Wells’s family and Ben Crump, the civil rights lawyer who is representing the family, have called for a federal investigation into Wells’s disappearance and death, after a Jackson county grand jury’s decision to decline to indict anyone in the case.
The Jackson county grand jury determined that Wells drowned. However, an independent autopsy conducted by the president of the Howard University hospital, Roger A Mitchell Jr, a forensic pathologist, determined there was no evidence of drowning due to the absence of water in Wells’s stomach, lungs and throat. That autopsy also noted bruising on Well’s head, back, left shoulder and buttocks.
“We do not believe Nolan drowned, and the blunt force trauma to his head cannot be ignored or explained away,” Crump said in a statement. “Nolan’s family deserves the truth, and we will keep fighting until every question is answered and justice is served.”
On Tuesday, Crump and Wells’s parents joined Cynthia Choi, Stop AAPI Hate’s executive director, in calling for a federal investigation into Wells’s death and disappearance. The California congresswoman Maxine Waters, the Florida congresswoman Frederica Wilson and others also sent a letter to Jessica Bowron, the acting director of the US National Park Service (NPS), noting that most of Horn Island is federally designated land and calling on the NPS’s investigative services branch to open a “prompt and exhaustive investigation” into Wells’s disappearance and death.
“Today, I am asking the people whose job it is to serve and protect to keep their word to our family,” Elmore Wonsley, Wells’s father, said at the press conference. “Our son was found on federal land, and we are asking the FBI to step in and do a full investigation. We’re not asking for special treatment. We’re asking for what any father would do for his child, and that’s to find the truth about what happened to his child.”
As he was leaving the White House, reporters asked Trump whether he planned to push the FBI to launch an independent investigation into Wells’s death.
“Well, we’re looking at that,” he said. “Yes, we are.”
“Sunday will mark 100 days since we have been looking into the death of Nolan Wells, so when President Trump responds to news reporters that ‘we’re looking into it’, we believe that carries more weight than the response given by the FBI,” Crump said in a statement. “Our team stands ready to work with the federal government to ensure Nolan’s death is investigated to the fullest extent.”

articles.title_orig: Thousands to march in Madrid after death of evicted pensioner Maricarmen
articles.title_zh: Thousands to march in Madrid after death of evicted pensioner Maricarmen
articles.content_orig:
Rally to remember woman, 87, whose rent battle with investment firm triggered nationwide protests over housing crisis
Thousands of people are expected to march through the centre of Madrid on Thursday evening in memory of María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her flat in the capital a fortnight before her death triggered mass protests over Spain’s housing crisis .
The pensioner, whose flat had been bought by an investment firm that sought to increase her rent by 230%, had become the public face of the crisis before her death in hospital on Wednesday night.
Abascal’s eviction unleashed waves of demonstrations across Spain, led to the setting up of a protest camp in the centre of the capital, and prompted the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to try to make the rental market more equitable. When those measures were voted down by rightwing and far-right parties last week, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, announced a snap general election , to be held on 29 November.
Anger over the plight of the woman who had become known around the country as Maricarmen remained undimmed a few hours after her death. On the pavement across from the apartment building where she had lived for seven decades, a steady stream of people visited a small, steadily growing memorial. Some came to light candles or leave flowers, while others left handwritten messages such as, “You made history Maricarmen,” and “Thank you for changing Spain”. Sara, 41, who had come with her young son and a sign that read, “Maricarmen, we’ll fight for you”, said: “We’re here because I think Maricarmen’s death shows how institutions can kill a person by failing to care for them.”
For many, the site was a reminder of all that Maricarmen had gone through as she tried to stay in her home, fending off three eviction attempts before the investment firm succeeded in forcing her out. “When people are protected less than investors, that leads to these kinds of things happening,” Sara added. “This woman could have died – if she had died of natural causes – she could have died peacefully in her home.”
Jaime, 34, pointed to all that Maricarmen had come to represent, particularly in a country like Spain, where social rights are supposedly guaranteed. “She had become a symbol, albeit one she never wanted to be, of the fight for decent housing,” he said. “So I came here because I think it’s important to restore some of the respect that Spanish society took away from Maricarmen.”
Visitors included some of the housing campaigners who had helped Maricarmen fight off previous eviction attempts. “This is really hard to take,” said Miguel, 59, fighting back tears as he added a red rose to the memorial. “When money is more powerful than people’s lives, it’s unbelievable.”
He said he hoped Maricarmen’s death would mark a turning point in Spain. “At least now we’re talking about this and putting names to those who are being evicted,” he said. “Because until now, there were 44 people a day being forced out of their homes. To the people in power, those are just numbers – now at least we’ve started putting names to those going through this.”
The Madrid tenants’ union announced a commemorative march at 8pm on Wednesday from the camp in the Puerta del Sol square to Abascal’s flat.
“Farewell, Maricarmen!” the union said in a post on social media . “Tonight we’ll honour you with a march … to the place that was your home for 70 years, and where you just wanted to stay until the end.”
Abascal’s ordeal has made housing a key issue in the forthcoming election, with Sánchez’s government seeking to push a redrafted package of measures through the council that operates when parliament has been dissolved. Meanwhile, the rightwing and far-right parties that opposed the legislation in congress last week have accused the prime minister of failing to act to address the housing crisis over the course of his eight years in office.
Sánchez offered his condolences to Abascal’s family and friends on Wednesday night. “A hug also to everyone who’s feeling this loss today as their own,” he wrote on social media. “Rest in peace.”
after newsletter promotion
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party (PP), which voted against last week’s emergency measures, also offered his condolences.
“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he wrote on social media. “When a person dies, there should be nothing but respect.”
The following day, however, Feijóo accused the government of trying to “manipulate the emotions of the Spanish people” by focusing on one particular eviction when there had been countless others during Sánchez’s time in office.
PP politicians also joined forces with the far right on Thursday to veto attempts to hold a minute’s silence for Maricarmen in Madrid’s regional parliament and the country’s senate. In Madrid’s municipal council, meanwhile, a rightwing attempt to block a minute’s silence was thwarted by opposition parties.
Abascal’s death has prompted reflection on how she had been treated by politicians and the media. The far-right Vox party, which also voted down the new decrees, had falsely suggested that Maricarmen would have had a home had she been an immigrant from North Africa , while one commentator had opined that “Maricarmen was chosen during a casting call for people facing eviction” to become a leftwing saint.
At least two far-right figures, including one of Vox’s MEPs, sought to sow doubt over the cause of Abascal’s death, with one even suggesting an autopsy should be carried out to determine whether the government had been involved . Another wrote : “Maricarmen was probably already made to send in her postal vote before they did her in. I expect anything from this scum.”

articles.title_orig: The Story Behind the Butterfly’s Enhanced Visual World of Color
articles.title_zh: The Story Behind the Butterfly’s Enhanced Visual World of Color
articles.content_orig:
Researchers discovered the genetic switch that produces extra light-detecting cells that led to the ability to recognize more colors in flowers and other butterflies
Many insects see the world through hundreds of tiny lenses that are grouped together in a visual organ known as the compound eye. Behind each lens sits a cluster of eight light-detecting cells arranged in a pattern that scientists believe has existed for hundreds of millions of years.
Butterflies are the rare exception. They are equipped with nine light-detecting cells, which gives them the ability to visually navigate a much richer world of color, compared with insects such as flies, and allows them to locate nectar and potential mates.
University of California San Diego scientists in School of Biological Sciences Associate Professor Michael Perry’s lab have discovered the genetic modification that gave butterflies this visual advantage.
“Butterflies see far more color than flies do because at some point in their evolution they added a photoreceptor to every unit of their compound eye — a rare break from an eye design that has otherwise been conserved across insects for hundreds of millions of years,” said Perry, a faculty member in the Department of Cell and Developmental Biology. “We found the genetic switch that did it.”
In a study published in the journal Science Advances , Perry and his coauthors identified the genetic steps involved in the emergence of the ninth photoreceptor in painted lady butterflies, the most widespread butterfly species in the world. While flies feature light-sensing cells known as photoreceptors R1-R8, butterflies expanded their color vision by adding a second R7 photoreceptor to each unit of the eye, the researchers found. To test whether that genetic change was enough on its own, they recreated it in a fruit fly — switching on a gene in cells that normally keeps it off, and timing it to the brief window when the eye is being built. This produced a “butterfly fly” that grows its eyes on the butterfly plan, with nine cells per eye unit instead of eight.
Antibody stains in a developing butterfly retina show that each unit eye contains two R7 color photoreceptors. Credit: Perry Lab, UC San Diego
A new light detector in the eye would be of no use if the brain is not able to connect to the new information provided by that detector. The scientists assumed that adding a sensory input such as a new photoreceptor unit should require the brain to slowly evolve a matching neuron partner that would receive information on the other end. That didn’t happen, the researchers found. To their surprise, no adaptive change was needed.
The fly brain regularly overproduces neurons that die off if they fail to find a connection. The brain of the butterfly-fly, they found, knew precisely how to handle the new photoreceptor by using its extra “standby” neurons and put them in play.
“When we gave those spare neurons something to connect to, they survived and wired up correctly — immediately — with no further genetic change,” said Perry. “In other words, the brain was ready before the eye asked. This is a rare, concrete case of evolution making use of neurons that were otherwise going to die.”
The new study’s findings provide a glimpse of how insects, with a flexible brain framework, were able to accommodate new inputs to evolutionarily adapt to an emerging need in their environment: an elevated ability to visualize flowering plants.
The team also found a hawkmoth that appears to be partway through the same transition: the lower half of its eye is butterfly-like, with two of these cells per unit, while the upper half is fly-like, with one. That is roughly what you would expect if the change began in one region of the eye and spread.
The research team is now exploring further unanswered questions, such as the difficult-to-study issue of whether the butterfly-fly can in fact see more vivid color with the additional photoreceptor, as butterflies do.
The research team included Ke Gao, Julia Ainsworth, Antoine Donati, Yunchong Zhao, Michelle Franc Ragsac, Cara Genduso, Zoie Andre, Andrew Tomlinson and Michael W. Perry. The researchers acknowledge support from: the National Institutes of Health (1T32GM133351); a Hellman Fellowship (Hellman Fellows Fund); a National Science Foundation CAREER award (2339031); and an NIH National Human Genome Research Institute grant (R01HG013634) from the EDGE program.

articles.title_orig: Google Cloud introduces Gemini agent for work as AI race heats up
articles.title_zh: Google Cloud introduces Gemini agent for work as AI race heats up
articles.content_orig:
Google on Thursday unveiled a new AI agent tailored for workplace tasks, positioning it to compete with other technology giants racing to offer their own virtual office assistants.
Called Gemini, the AI is a "universal agent" that can write and run code, create images and media and integrate with Google products like Gmail, Docs, Drive and Sheets, as well as third-party apps like Slack and Microsoft 365, Google said in its statement .
Thomas Kurian, the CEO of Google Cloud, shared the new product during a keynote address at Gemini at Work 2026 on Thursday, an annual event where Google showcases its suite of AI technology.
Google said the agent can seamlessly integrate into people's workflow, acting like a co-worker that can carry out tasks autonomously. Workers can delegate tasks to the agent, and it will return a finished product, Kurian said in the company's blog post.
"Gemini can function as your personal assistant or as a team member, where it works on behalf of a group of people, like a project manager within a team, or on behalf of a specific role in an organization, like an analyst in your finance department," he wrote.
To execute on certain tasks, Gemini can create its own "sub-agents," which Google described as "temporary, job-specific agents, each with their own identity," that can work together to accomplish goals over several days.
The AI agent, which runs in the Cloud, is designed to build memory and skills based on the tasks it's assigned and the questions users ask it.
"You never have to re-brief it or wonder which machine you told it to do something on," Kurian wrote in the blog post.
Gemini joins a growing field of AI agents marketed for personal and workplace use. In September, Meta introduced Muse , a personal AI assistant that has been downloaded millions of times. OpenAI followed suit late last month with the introduction of "Dots" , an "AI helper" available to ChatGPT users with Pro and Business Premium accounts.

articles.title_orig: ‘I just want to hold him’: USS Lincoln sailor to meet his 10-month-old son as ship docks
articles.title_zh: ‘I just want to hold him’: USS Lincoln sailor to meet his 10-month-old son as ship docks
articles.content_orig:
After more than 300 days at sea, the USS Abraham Lincoln is finally come back home to San Diego. NBC 7’s Dana Williams reports.
Among the thousands of family members awaiting to greet their loved ones as they step off the USS Abraham Lincoln will be 10-month-old Nathan, who is meeting his father for the first time.
Brent Ledbetter is an air traffic control center officer aboard the aircraft carrier. His son was born in November, about a week after Ledbetter reported to the ship, NBC News reported.
Stream San Diego News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC 7.
"I just want to hold him, play with him,” Ledbetter told NBC News. “He’s crawling around now, so I’m excited to chase him around the house and give him all the love that, that, you know — have been kind of withheld for the last 10 months. I’m so excited."
Ledbetter told NBC News his wife is also an air traffic control officer and had been assigned to the Lincoln. He replaced her on the ship shortly before she gave birth.
Among the roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines onboard the Lincoln, there are more than 50 babies waiting for a parent’s return on Thursday when the ship docks at Naval Air Station North Island.
What began as a Pacific deployment with a spring return soon shifted to a prolonged stay at sea as the carrier was diverted to Middle East to support the U.S. and Israel's war with Iran. Over the next several months, the crew would endure deployment extensions, supply shortages and deteriorating mental health.
Now, after nearly a year at sea, the beleaguered Lincoln is almost home and crewmembers who are parents will be among the first allowed off the ship.

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike now walking after US execution went wrong, lawyer says
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike now walking after US execution went wrong, lawyer says
articles.content_orig:
Christa Pike is "up and walking" though mentally "foggy" while in hospital after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, her legal team says.
Pike, 50, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September. Experts described it as unprecedented.
Speaking late on Wednesday to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, lawyer Stephen Ferrell said he had not spoken to Pike directly but had learned her arms were swollen and barely functioning as she took her first steps around her hospital room.
A court has ordered state officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution.
That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.
The Pike case is now in uncharted territory, as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
The failed execution was branded a "mess" by the mother of Slemmer, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death.
Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's gruesome murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.
Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
In their previous updates on Pike's condition after the attempted execution, her team had said she was awake and speaking, and experiencing anger and confusion. She was said at that stage to be handcuffed to her bed.
Her lawyer Randy Spivey said after Wednesday's court hearing: "She cannot move either of her arms." He added: "Both of her arms and hands are tremendously swollen, and we do not know what if any function she will regain in her arms."
In the later updates, given on Wednesday to the BBC, Ferrell said Pike was continuing to experience the after-effects of the drug pentobarbital.
The drug was injected into her body in two doses by prison staff during the scheduled execution on 30 September. But once it became clear that Pike was not going to die from the execution attempt, she was taken to hospital, where she was initially unconscious and declared to be in a critical condition.
As of late on Wednesday, though, Pike was "fairly well", Ferrell said.
"What's been described to me is that physically there's quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured and she's not able to use them very much."
Of her physical movements, Ferrell added: "She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, not very far."
Turning to her mental state, he said: "I think it's kind of good and bad. Good that she is fairly with it, but she's also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily and forgets where she's going."
Ferrell said much remained unknown about what happens next. "I assume [the situation for Pike] will keep improving, but there could be some permanent damage. We don't know that yet."
He added that the team wanted Pike to receive psychological support, since that "clearly is necessary now".
Ferrell and his colleagues - who highlighted ahead of the attempted execution that Pike had a condition that would make the injection method difficult - oppose any new attempt by state prison authorities to follow the same approach.
They are also calling on the state governor, Bill Lee, to downgrade Pike's punishment to the lesser sentence of life in prison without parole.
Meanwhile, Tennessee's proponents of capital punishment have suggested that a different method be used. Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for state governor in next month's election, said: "Bring back the electric chair."
Asked during a court hearing on Wednesday whether the state intended to reschedule Pike's execution, the state's attorney general said he did not know.
For now, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions in the state for the rest of the year, and has said he wants answers about what went wrong. The state's prisons chief is resigning after the failed execution.
Wednesday's court hearing related to the preservation of evidence following the first attempt.
The judge, I'Ashea Myles, ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, like packaging, inserts, and labels.
The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition prior to, during and after the 30 September execution attempt.
She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.
Correction 8 October: This article originally said that Pike and her boyfriend had first met Colleen Slemmer at a job training camp for "troubled teens". This has been amended to make clear that the scheme was for low-income youths aged 16 to 24 and was not specifically for troubled teenagers.

articles.title_orig: ‘The Floating World’ by Ben Eastham, Reviewed
articles.title_zh: ‘The Floating World’ by Ben Eastham, Reviewed
articles.content_orig:
For all its suspicion of the contemporary artworld and its machinations, the art critic’s debut novel remains surprisingly sincere about art itself
The unnamed narrator of Ben Eastham’s debut novel, The Floating World , is, like Eastham himself , an art critic. Grieving his recently deceased wife, he feels lost while teaching at a school where the students refer to him as ‘Doctor Pissington’. Then a friend offers him a job back in the artworld. He is to work on ‘The Floating World’, which is ‘a gated community beneath a giant dome on a desert island’ being built by a tech billionaire for the wealthiest as a refuge from climate crisis and political collapse. Our morally conflicted protagonist is hired to conduct research for an art exhibition marking the island’s inauguration. The novel negotiates the contradiction of inhabiting a contemporary artworld sustained by the good intentions of art workers who align themselves with beauty and virtue, while depending on the very forces their work purports to resist.
It opens with the narrator, in Ireland, on the verge of writing, before disappearing into his recollections, and eventually returns to the point at which the story is being written (more on which later). Grief provides its emotional landscape: the narrator’s reality is shot through with the frenetic despair that comes with the sudden loss of his wife. His grief gradually becomes entangled with the project of ‘The Floating World’ and the people making it, forcing a confrontation with the loss he has been carrying. It is in such experiences that resist ordinary expression that art becomes most meaningful: a painting, for example, that is ‘a truth that didn’t need explaining. No aristocrats, no symbolism, no lies. A painting clear as love’; and another, when the narrator’s friend likens the experience of pregnancy to a painting they once saw in a museum, in which ‘The colours are stronger and brighter, there’s a texture. It’s like breaking through a screen, the world feels bigger, like it can’t be contained.’
Eastham is at his most sensitive when criticism itself becomes inadequate. There is a pleasing irony in an art critic writing about an art critic for whom, and for the artists around him, the most profound encounters with art seem to occur precisely when interpretation fails. While Eastham is tender in his descriptions of art, his acute observations of the people surrounding it can be lacerating. He has a formidable talent for summoning up a character – or skewering one – in a sentence. One woman possesses ‘the erotic hauteur of an academic who in her youth danced beneath filtered spotlights at psychedelic happenings’. Another, ‘a woman in those oversized metal-rimmed spectacles designed to signal to civilians that the wearer is an intellectual’. Eastham is exacting not only when it comes to how people appear, but also about the identities they are trying, sometimes desperately, to project. Despite the grieving anguish of its narrator, it is his wry, deadpan humour that carries the novel. There is a dryly comic sparring match with a ‘philanthropist’ who believes happiness can be quantified, and a conversation between partygoers about where, literally, ‘the shit is going’. At times it is not unlike a drawing-room comedy, with its sharp wit, back-and-forth banter and clever insults.
The metafictional frame allows the novel to avoid the aftermath of its most dramatic events, dwelling instead on the act of remembering and reconstructing them. I’m not convinced this framing adds to the reader’s understanding of the narrator’s grief or the events being recounted. The narrator returns to remarkably similar emotional terrain at the end: melancholic and still lost, but perhaps slightly more hopeful for the future. For all its suspicion of the contemporary artworld and its machinations, The Floating World remains surprisingly sincere about art itself. This is especially persuasive when Eastham uses art to give shape to experiences that elude explanation – love, pregnancy, grief – reminding us that beneath the bullshit posturing of the artworld is an unexpectedly earnest faith that art can make felt what we cannot quite articulate.
The Floating World by Ben Eastham. Fitzcarraldo Editions , £14.99 (softcover)

articles.title_orig: At Texas Rally, Trump and Paxton Make for an Awkward Pair
articles.title_zh: At Texas Rally, Trump and Paxton Make for an Awkward Pair
articles.content_orig:
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage
Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections
Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally was rocked by repeated protests on Wednesday as the US president urged Texas voters to back the embattled Senate candidate Ken Paxton.
At least half a dozen demonstrators interrupted the US president during his remarks in San Antonio, with some led away by police. One was physically assaulted by an older Trump supporter as he tried to leave the arena.
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage. “He’s going back home to mom,” the president said after the man was removed. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”
Supporters waving cowboy hats and chanting “USA” drowned out some of the protesters, while Trump told demonstrators to “get the hell out of here”. He mocked their appearance and claimed without evidence that “they’re paid by enemies of our nation”.
The president also used Wednesday’s rally to address recent comments in which he appeared to suggest that Iran could destroy Los Angeles or San Diego, earning widespread condemnation from Democrats.
In remarks that were again less than crystal clear, Trump said: “I said it the other day, let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. Let them hit – you want to see a horror show? You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles and you want to see some bad things happen.
“You want to see a country that would be in freefall. We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities, we protect our country, we’re not letting that happen. And they’d use it, too. They’d use it.”
Trump was making his third trip to Texas in less than a month as Republicans pour money into races they had expected to win comfortably in November’s midterm elections.
Paxton, whom Trump endorsed during the Republican primary after turning against the incumbent senator John Cornyn, was called on stage by the president and thanked him for his support.
“Mr President, I want to thank you for coming for me, for coming for us, and for coming for Texas,” Paxton said. “We are going to win this race.”
Trump described Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America”, and said: “He was tough and he was with us all the way. He’s a fantastic man.”
The Republican campaign to maintain control of the Senate has become increasingly focused on Texas, where Democrat James Talarico has emerged as a serious threat. A New York Times/Siena College poll released last weekend showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Texas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988.
Trump won the state by almost 14 percentage points in 2024, but his approval rating has fallen sharply. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday put his approval rating at 32%, while registered voters preferred Democrats to Republicans 44%-37%.
after newsletter promotion
Trump’s relationship with Paxton has sometimes appeared uneasy. Trump called Paxton “a pain in the ass sometimes” last week, but on Wednesday did not discuss a leaked recording of Paxton in which the Senate candidate reportedly complained about the war in Iran, rising fuel prices and the way his campaign was being run.
Instead he spent much of the rally attacking Talarico, whom he repeatedly referred to as “Tala-freako”. He claimed without evidence that Talarico is vegan and recently disappeared: “He’s sick because he’s been forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.”
Trump insisted: “The people of Texas are not going to let weak, gutless, self-hating, transgender-promoting freak shows destroy everything that we’ve built.”
The president’s political difficulties in Texas were underlined by the absence of the Republican governor, Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is himself facing a competitive re-election race against the Democratic state representative Gina Hinojosa.
Abbott was instead due to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on his decision not to appear with Trump.
Republicans have now devoted more than $300m to elections in Texas, according to the Associated Press, while Trump’s broader 32-day campaign blitz has taken him through several Republican-leaning states, including Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska.

articles.title_orig: Ex-prince Andrew search warrants quashed after police accept legal error
articles.title_zh: Ex-prince Andrew search warrants quashed after police accept legal error
articles.content_orig:
Thames Valley Police has accepted warrants it used to search Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's homes at the time of his arrest in February were unlawful, the High Court has been told.
Following Thursday's hearing, items seized in the raid continue to be held by the police, with a further hearing to take place in 2027 to decide whether the material can be used as evidence.
Meanwhile, the criminal investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is ongoing.
The former prince, who denies any wrongdoing, was arrested by police on 19 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after which he launched a legal challenge over the legality of the search warrants.
The force said it accepted that the "initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect" before they searched the properties.
On Thursday at the High Court, judge Mr Justice Hilliard said Mountbatten-Windsor and the police had agreed that the search warrants had been unlawful.
However, he added: "The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful."
Mountbatten-Windsor opposes the police's bid to retain the evidence, the judge said, and another hearing is expected in 2027.
His lawyers have used a judicial review to challenge the actions of the force's chief constable and the Central Criminal Court in the build-up to his arrest.
His arrest arose after the US Department of Justice published documents which raised suspicions he had forwarded confidential information to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein when Mountbatten-Windsor was a UK trade envoy in 2010.
He has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.
The court heard on Thursday that Thames Valley Police seized documents and electronic devices when they raided Mountbatten-Windsor's homes earlier this year.
Thames Valley Police's position was that they had applied for search warrants under section eight and nine of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 at a hearing at the Central Criminal Court the day before the search.
That court determined that only section eight search warrants were needed and they were granted on that basis - but subsequently, a legal challenge has established that the court should have issued them under the section nine.
The judge explained on Thursday why the police could keep hold of the former prince's items that had been seized.
He said: "There would be little point in handing property back if it could then simply be lawfully seized under some other provision."
A Thames Valley Police spokesperson said: "The agreement that led to the quashing of the warrants relates specifically to a decision made by the court regarding the legal basis for these and is not a judgement on our ongoing investigation.
"We ensured the court was presented with all the necessary information and paperwork to inform their decision, following the correct legal processes throughout.
"We accept the position that the initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed.
"Legal proceedings are currently ongoing to decide how material seized during the searches will be managed and whether we can lawfully retain it in support of our ongoing investigation."
The force said its "investigation into alleged misconduct in public office by a man in his 60s from Norfolk remains ongoing, and we continue to pursue all reasonable lines of enquiry to effectively and fairly progress this investigation".
The next stage in this legal dispute will be a behind-closed-doors hearing over whether the police can still retain material seized from Mountbatten-Windsor's homes under alternative powers designed for situations like this.
The error that has led to Thames Valley Police accepting the search warrants were unlawful relates to the particular power the judge permitted the force to use when its officers raided the properties.
Strict legal safeguards on searches bar the police from automatically seizing sensitive material without thinking through in advance the need to take it.
Examples of that material include advice from a suspect's lawyer or material which does not really belong to them, such as copies of confidential work-related papers from an employer.
In practice, if the police find such material during a search, they should return it rather than use it in their investigation.
The category of search warrant that was granted by the court in this instance did not take into account the possibility of such protected material being seized.
However, the law says police can in fact seize that kind of material - or potentially retain it in the event of an error - providing they pass some extra tests.
Thames Valley Police must now convince a judge that the material is likely to be of "substantial value" to their investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor and, ultimately, potential evidence to present to a court.
So while the force has conceded the search warrant was unlawful, a judge will have to decide whether this alternative search power, with its extra safeguards, justifies them keeping and using the material after all.

articles.title_orig: Amazon’s new Alexa Tablets are an iPad-inspired reboot, complete with the Play Store
articles.title_zh: Amazon’s new Alexa Tablets are an iPad-inspired reboot, complete with the Play Store
articles.content_orig:
Amazon has an all-new lineup of tablets ready to tempt you this holiday season, and for once, you might actually want to buy them. While the company has tried in previous years to make an upmarket play for relevancy in the tablet space, these new Alexa Tablets — RIP “Fire” — have the one thing everyone’s wanted for years: actual Play Store support.
Yes, a decade after ditching the “Kindle” branding in its tablet lineup, Amazon is ditching the Fire brand entirely for its new lineup of iPad competitors. That’s not me trying to write off its Android-powered rivals; rather, the sizes and designs all make for devices that, frankly, look like iPad knock-offs. Alexa Tablets come in three sizes: an 8-inch entry-level iPad Mini competitor, an 11-inch base iPad-esque slate, and a 12-inch “Pro” model that looks to be the most unique of the bunch. They’re all designed with aluminum bodies and, despite being much more expensive than the Fire tablets they’re replacing, still manage to undercut most of the market.
The 8.7-inch 60Hz Alexa Tablet 8 features 4GB of RAM, up to 128GB of storage, and comes in graphite, rosette, and teal, while the 90Hz 11-inch Alexa Tablet 11 features 8GB of RAM, up to 128GB of storage, and adds matcha and amethyst to the mix. Both run on a MediaTek 8189 8-core processor, a relatively recent chipset that appeared in a handful of seemingly-unreleased ChromeOS devices over the past year or so, before landing in these budget tablets. While I wouldn’t say there’s much to write home here about the specs — and again, the design is just absolutely a blatant copy of the iPad — it certainly sounds like a big upgrade over their predecessors.
And really, that comes down to the software. Despite Amazon’s current Android-less strategy on its Fire TV devices , the company seems to be doubling down on Android with its tablets. While it does have a unique launcher designed to push Alexa+, these things run proper Android, complete with the Play Store front and center on the device. YouTube is one of the highlighted apps on their store listings, and as someone who maintained Play Store sideloading guides at two different tech websites over the past decade, I can certainly say I never saw it coming. I have no idea how the actual software experience will feel day-to-day, but in terms of app support, it’s one problem that’s finally solved.
The star of the show, of course, is the 12-inch Alexa Tablet 12 Pro . This is, bar none, the most premium tablet Amazon has ever shipped, with a price that matches. It combines a 2.8K 3:2 120Hz display with quad speakers, 8GB of RAM, 128GB of storage, and a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor. That’s a real processor, and while I wouldn’t say it’s worthy of being called a flagship chipset, it’s undoubtedly the most powerful chip Amazon’s ever used. It’s a good sign when you’re using the same processor that a budget gaming-focused brand like Poco used just a year or two ago.
The 12-inch model also comes in an optional “nanomatte” version for an anti-glare experience, which also allows you to upgrade your RAM and storage to 16GB and 256GB, respectively. 16GB of RAM in an Amazon tablet — it’s a new day after all. And like its last attempt to go full-premium, the company does offer optional stylus and keyboard accessories for road warriors on a budget.
The Alexa Tablet 8 starts at $230 for the base 64GB model with lockscreen ads, or $250 without, while the Alexa Tablet 11 starts at $330 for its base model, or $350 for the ad-free version. Both feature a 128GB upgrade for $50 more. The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro starts at $500 for the base 128GB model; the nanomatte upgrade will run you $50 more. Meanwhile, that high-end 16/256 variant costs a whopping $680, and while that might sound pretty expensive on paper, it comes in well under Samsung’s latest 12-inch tablet for anyone who doesn’t need that level of processing power. Oh, and absolutely no ads on any of the 12 Pro models — the price you see is the price you pay, no upgrades necessary.

articles.title_orig: Psychedelic Paintings by Rafael Silveira Explore a World of ‘Visual Synonymies’
articles.title_zh: Psychedelic Paintings by Rafael Silveira Explore a World of ‘Visual Synonymies’
articles.content_orig:
Flowers for eyes, a horizon for a mouth… a popsicle for a holy relic? Rafael Silveira has long been interested in what he describes as “visual synonymies,” which he likens to “formal correspondences between seemingly unrelated things, moments in which one image unexpectedly recognizes itself in another.” The Brazilian artist’s surreal paintings replace facial features with landforms, flora, and fauna, sometimes hybridizing animals, figures, and other objects.
The works seen here were recently included in the artist’s solo exhibition Popsicledelic Trip at KP Projects Gallery in Los Angeles alongside a show by Silveira’s wife, the artist Flávia Itiberê . A series of vertical pieces with ornate, hand-carved wooden frames resemble the silhouette of popsicles, while figures hold giant versions of the frozen treats in a stylistic nod to religious art during the Renaissance .
The popsicle may seem like a quirky, even out-of-place reference within the context of these works, but for Silveira, the objects represent the broader idea that everything in the universe is connected. No matter how absurd it may seem at first glance—a man with a tree for a head or ice cream cones floating planet-like in a starry sky—the point is that they all really do exist simultaneously. Silveira juxtaposes objects and organisms in unlikely scenarios to challenge how we perceive the world around us and how even the same shape can have completely different associations.
One compositional form in particular, the tavola centinata , describes the shape of a canvas or relief with a squared base and rounded top. A feature commonly found in Gothic and early Renaissance paintings, it has the same silhouette as a classic popsicle. In a statement, Silveira says:
The connection is at once surprising and inevitable. One belongs to the sacred history of painting; the other to the realm of the ephemeral, the popular, the sweet, the melting. Bringing them together creates a bridge between devotional form and unstable matter, between permanence and disappearance, between the spiritual weight of the altarpiece and the fragile delight of something destined to dissolve.

articles.title_orig: Odyssey Launches Odyssey-3, Its Most Powerful Foundation World Model Built to Power AI Across the Physical World
articles.title_zh: Odyssey Launches Odyssey-3, Its Most Powerful Foundation World Model Built to Power AI Across the Physical World
articles.content_orig:
Odyssey Launches Odyssey-3, Its Most Powerful Foundation World Model Built to Power AI Across the Physical World
New model demonstrates a shared understanding of the world across robots, humanoids, vehicles, drones, AI agents, and video games
Odyssey , an AI research company pioneering foundation world models, today announced Odyssey-3, its most powerful world model to date. The new model represents a significant advance toward general-purpose intelligence that can understand, predict, and interact with both physical and virtual environments.
This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261008756684/en/
Caption: Odyssey’s latest world model powering Flexion’s robot. Credit: Odyssey
World models learn from vast examples of the world evolving to predict and simulate what happens next, including how actions affect outcomes. Odyssey-3 gives intelligent systems a general understanding of how the world works before they are taught a specific task. The model has shown the ability to control robots and humanoids, drive vehicles, pilot drones, generate environments for training AI agents, and play video games. The new model has already been adopted by companies including Flexion, a leader in humanoid autonomy.
Trained on a vast dataset of visual observations of the world, Odyssey-3 builds on world models the company has been developing over the past three years. It has learned representations of physics, dynamics, cause and effect, and human behavior that can be applied across physical and virtual systems.
Using this pretrained foundation, Odyssey-3 enables physical agents: intelligent systems that can apply a shared understanding of the world across different machines, environments, and tasks. Rather than learning every new task entirely from scratch, these systems can draw on a broader model of how the world works and adapt that knowledge to new situations with relatively little additional experience.
“Odyssey-3 is a big step toward a single intelligence that can understand and operate in the world around us,” said Oliver Cameron, co-founder and CEO of Odyssey . “World models give physical agents a foundation of knowledge they can carry from one machine, environment, or task to another. We believe that the ability to learn broadly and then adapt with relatively little experience is the path toward increasingly general physical intelligence.”
The company has demonstrated Odyssey-3 across six domains:
Odyssey-3 is designed as a foundation that can span these domains rather than a model optimized for a single machine or application. By learning common representations of how environments behave and how actions change them, Odyssey is working toward world models that can transfer knowledge across increasingly diverse physical and virtual systems.
Odyssey is an AI lab pioneering general world models: causal, multimodal systems that learn to predict and interact with the world over long horizons. This foundational technology promises to revolutionize robotics, science, healthcare, education, gaming, defense, and beyond.
Odyssey’s founders previously pioneered one of the most complex applications of physical AI: self-driving cars. They’ve since brought together a world-class research team from DeepMind, Tesla, Waymo, Meta, Apple, and Wayve, whose members have contributed to language models, video models, world models and autonomous systems, including DeepMind Gemini, DeepMind Veo, Wayve GAIA and Tesla FSD.
Media: media@odyssey.systems
