articles.title_orig: World Sight Day: Restoring sight where cataract surgery is scarce
articles.title_zh: World Sight Day: Restoring sight where cataract surgery is scarce
articles.content_orig:
Lloyd Williams, MD, PhD, discusses rising cataract blindness and low-cost surgery in conflict zones for World Sight Day.
Cataract remains a leading cause of vision impairment and blindness worldwide. At least 2.2 billion people have a near or distance vision impairment, and in at least 1 billion of those cases, the impairment could have been prevented or has yet to be addressed, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Cataract accounts for 94 million of those cases, and 1 in 2 people who need cataract surgery do not have access to it.¹
World Sight Day is an annual day of awareness held on the second Thursday of October and coordinated by the International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness (IAPB). This year, it falls on October 8. The 2026 #LoveYourEyes campaign centers on personal stories, lived experiences, and community action ahead of the first Global Summit for Eye Health on November 2 in Antigua and Barbuda.²
To mark the occasion, Lloyd Williams, MD, PhD , director of Duke Global Ophthalmology at Duke Eye Center in Durham, North Carolina, spoke with Ophthalmology Times about why cataract blindness continues to rise and how teams deliver high-quality surgery in low-resource settings. Williams received the American Academy of Ophthalmology's 2025 Outstanding Humanitarian Service Award for expanding access to cataract and corneal surgery in underserved regions.
Williams attributed the increase to aging populations in regions where ophthalmic care has not expanded, compounded by conflict and poverty that make many areas harder to reach. He cited a recent cataract camp in South Sudan.
"We literally had to negotiate a ceasefire in order to do cataract surgery," Williams told Ophthalmology Times .
Williams highlighted several organizations working to expand access to eye care. Readers can donate or get involved through the following: • Duke Global Ophthalmology: Give to Duke GO .³ • Cure Blindness Project: Donate ; ophthalmologists and practices can also join its Global Partners Program.⁴ • IAPB: Individuals can become a Love Your Eyes Visionary , and organizations can apply for membership .⁵ • CBM (Christian Blind Mission): Donate .⁶ • Sightsavers: Donate or fundraise through Sightsavers USA.⁷
On a recent trip to Abyei, surgery cost approximately $70 per case using manual small incision cataract surgery (MSICS), which requires a microscope as the only electrical equipment. In skilled hands, Williams said, MSICS achieves results roughly equivalent to those in the US. A $700,000 donation this year is expected to fund approximately 9000 surgeries, a volume he said would not be possible with phacoemulsification or laser-based approaches.
"I strongly believe that we're not providing somebody substandard care," Williams said.
Williams also addressed studies linking cataract surgery to lower rates of dementia diagnosis, which cannot yet establish cause and effect. He recalled veterans whose anxiety and depression appeared to improve after surgery during his residency, and he said he discusses the cognitive benefits of sight with families of older patients. Reflecting on his own vision problem as a resident, he described sight as "something that you could lose just like your arm."

articles.title_orig: Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped while repairing campaign sign
articles.title_zh: Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped while repairing campaign sign
articles.content_orig:
Warning: This article contains details which some readers may find distressing.
A congressional candidate in Arizona has said she was raped in a car park as she repaired campaign signs late at night in her district.
Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a Democrat, told the Phoenix New Times she was knocked unconscious during the alleged attack in the Phoenix suburb of Sun City on 14 August, waking up to find a man on top of her.
She said she did not initially notify police until filing a report with the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office two weeks later.
Her Republican opponent, Abraham Hamadeh, urged authorities in a statement to "investigate these serious allegations thoroughly, including finding all possible camera footage of the time and place".
"No American should become a victim of a crime in their own community," said Hamadeh, who is running for a second term in office.
Greene-Placentia told the Phoenix New Times she was "embarrassed" and "just wanted to forget", but felt compelled stand up for other victims.
The candidate said she often speaks on the campaign trail about fighting for Arizonans.
She told the Phoenix New Times: "I didn't feel like I could keep saying that if I weren't also fighting for women that are victims of sexual assault."
The BBC has contacted the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office for comment. A sheriff's spokesman told the New York Times the investigation was ongoing.
After the attack, Greene-Placentia said she withdrew from the public for two days, staying in an apartment separate from her husband and skipping a campaign event.
When she emerged, her husband, campaign staff and others in her circle noticed she was acting differently, according to Phoenix New Times.
Greene-Placentia said she did not see a doctor following the alleged attack in congressional district eight and did not receive a sexual assault examination.
She said her memory of what happened was spotty and she did not get a good look at either of the two assailants, but described them as white men, according to the New York Times.
She told the Phoenix New Times that one assailant may have made a comment about her political affiliation, together with a misogynistic slur, although she could not be certain.
The candidate said she was concerned voters might think it was a political stunt to win points in a heavily Republican district. She also expressed concern that the allegations might overshadow her messaging around affordability.
If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide .

articles.title_orig: New GETI publication explores future of Christian unity
articles.title_zh: New GETI publication explores future of Christian unity
articles.content_orig:
A new publication from the World Council of Churches (WCC) Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation (EEF) brings together the voices and theological reflections of young ecumenists from around the world who attended the 2025 edition of the WCC Global Ecumenical Theological Institute (GETI). It brings fresh inputs to the pressing question for the churches today: Where now for visible unity?
From left: Rev. Prof. Dr Meehyun Chung, moderator of the WCC Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation; Prof. Dr Ani Ghazaryan Drissi, WCC programme executive for Ecumenical Theological Education and coordinator of GETI 2025; Rev. Dr Nathan Digby, GETI 2025 facilitator and member of the WCC Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation; during the launch event of the GETI 2025 book on 8 October.
“ GETI 2025: Voices and Visions of Transformative Unity,” edited by Prof. Dr Ani Ghazaryan Drissi and Rev. Prof. Teddy Chalwe Sakupapa, emerges from the WCC ’ s 4th GETI, held in the context of the Sixth World Conference on Faith and Order in Wadi El Natrun, Egypt. The publication, launched on 8 October, during the biannual meeting of the EEF Commission, comes at a significant moment.
“ The fruits of ecumenical dialogue must take root in the lives of our churches,” said Ghazaryan. “ The GETI 2025 message brought this bold challenge to the Sixth World Conference on Faith and Order and the wider ecumenical movement: let the unity we confess become the life we share.”
This publication carries that call forward, she added, through voices and visions rooted in different churches, cultures, and lived realities. “ Their theological reflections invite us to ask how the fruits of ecumenical dialogue can shape our communities, deepen our relationships, and renew our common witness,” said Ghazaryan. “ They call us to listen more deeply, confront exclusion, and share responsibility for the future of our churches.”
Bossey students who took part of GETI 2025 shared their testimonies during the launch event.
The volume presents a global and contextually grounded exploration of Christian unity. Its contributors reflect on reception, Nicaea, pilgrimage, trust and companionship, while also addressing colonial wounds, trauma, migration, ethnic violence, Palestine, digital ecumenism, and ecological crisis.
Rather than treating unity as an abstract theological ideal, the book emphasizes unity as something that must be embodied through relationships, truth-telling, healing, solidarity, and public witness. Its concluding message describes young ecumenists as contributors to the present and future of the ecumenical movement.
GETI 2025 facilitator and EEF commissioner Rev. Dr Nathan Digby explained that a central goal of the WCC ’ s Ecumenical Theological Education work is to provide opportunities for emerging ecumenical leaders to be formed in ecumenism and to ensure that their voices are heard, encouraged, and shared with the wider church.
“ The publication of GETI 2025: Voices and Visions for Transformative Unity gives concrete expression to this commitment,” he said. “ As part of their theological formation, students participating in GETI 2025 developed academic papers exploring the theme of visible Christian unity in relation to their own theological interests, contexts, and experiences.”
This volume recognizes and celebrates their intellectual and theological work while creating a platform through which their perspectives can contribute to broader conversations about the future of Christian unity, added Digby.
“ By bringing these emerging voices together in one publication, GETI 2025: Voices and Visions for Transformative Unity not only documents an important dimension of the GETI experience but also invests in the next generation of ecumenical thinkers and leaders, whose insights and visions are essential for shaping a more transformative and visible unity among Christians.”
Published by WCC Publications, the book offers churches, theological institutions, students, and ecumenical partners a rich resource for reflection and conversation on the future of Christian unity.
The session also included the presentation of the GETI Visual Report and a short video featuring voices and moments of GETI 2025.
The EEF Commission is meeting at the WCC Ecumenical Institute at Bossey 4-9 October.

articles.title_orig: A Rare Image of Mars at Dawn Reveals the Beauty of Its Ancient Cliffs
articles.title_zh: A Rare Image of Mars at Dawn Reveals the Beauty of Its Ancient Cliffs
articles.content_orig:
The captivating shapes of wind-carved crags called yardangs are revealed in this zoomed-in crop of a broader panorama captured by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover on Aug. 11, 2026. Scientists are eager to learn more about how the yardang layer formed.
Sunlight illuminates wind-carved cliffs in a dramatic new image.
A newly released panorama captured by NASA’s Curiosity rover offers the most detailed view yet of distant, wind-carved Martian cliffs, highlighting features the mission’s scientists have long been waiting to see up close. The scene was snapped at 8:30 a.m. local Mars time, showing striking blue hues in the foreground as bright morning light illuminates crags known as yardangs on the horizon.
The panorama was captured by Curiosity’s Mastcam on Aug. 11, the 4,982nd Martian day, or sol, of the mission, and comprises six individual images that were stitched together after being sent to Earth. Unlike most of Curiosity’s Mastcam images, this one was processed without white balancing, preserving the early morning appearance.
The six shots that make up this panorama, captured by NASA’s Curiosity on Aug. 11, were stitched together after being sent back to Earth. Unlike most images from the rover’s Mastcam, this one was processed without the usual white balancing — an artistic choice that preserves the early morning appearance.
The yardang layer extends roughly 10 miles (16 kilometers) across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that Curiosity has been ascending since 2014. In fact, the rover recently passed another milestone in its ascent, reaching 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) of elevation — the most ever climbed on Mars. As it draws ever-closer to the yardangs, mission scientists expect to get even more amazing imagery — and, they hope, answers to how these cliffs were created.
Mount Sharp is made up of layers, each recording a distinct period of Mars’ history. By studying them, scientists have been able to learn more about lakes and streams that covered this part of the Red Planet billions of years ago. Eventually, the water dried up and left salty minerals behind. After new material stopped settling on the mountain, some of it may have been stripped away by wind, giving rise to the yardangs.
This artist’s concept shows Mount Sharp, the 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that NASA’s Curiosity has been ascending since 2014. The location of the yardang layer, which the rover recently captured from a distance, is indicated by an ellipse annotation on the mountain’s northwestern shoulder.
NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover captured this view looking back at the floor of Gale Crater on Sept. 5, 2026. Just nine days prior, the rover had marked 1 kilometer of elevation gain above the crater floor since beginning its ascent of Mount Sharp in 2014.
“The yardang layer looks out of place. It’s the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on,” said Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity project scientist of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “But that’s what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions.”
Curiosity is in the second year of its fifth extended mission, which started with an exploration of the spiderweb-like boxwork ridges . The rover will spend most of the next year or so driving through layers enriched with sulfates and carbonates, both signs of ancient drying on the surface. Sometime in 2027, scientists hope to reach the base of the yardangs, where Curiosity will be able to use its robotic arm to collect one-of-a-kind data on these mysterious features.

NASA JPL leads the mission on behalf of the agency’s Science Mission Directorate in Washington as part of its Mars Exploration Program portfolio. Malin Space Science Systems in San Diego built and operates Mastcam.

articles.title_orig: Amoris laetitia: Pastoral experiences in Asia and challenges of digital world
articles.title_zh: Amoris laetitia: Pastoral experiences in Asia and challenges of digital world
articles.content_orig:
Families today are âa challenging mosaic of diverse realities, marked by joys, hopes, struggles and wounds. The family is not only a place to which the Church brings the Gospel. It is also a place from which the Gospel comes alive â from one generation to another, from one family to another, and from families to society.â
Cardinal Filipe Neri Ferrão, Metropolitan Archbishop of Goa and Daman, opened his address with this reflection at the start of the second day of Pope Leo XIVâs meeting with the heads of the Eastern Churches and the presidents of the Bishopsâ Conferences, ten years after Amoris laetitia .
The Indian Cardinal addressed the theme âFamilies today: reality, beauty and challenges. Discerning the signs of the times through the experience of families and the Churchâs pastoral commitment today.â
He invited participants in the meeting, conducted in a synodal style, to ask themselves in their discernment: âWhat is the Holy Spirit asking the Church to change?â
This concerned ânot only in what we do for the families, but in how we understand, accompany and empower them as protagonists of the Gospel and as enduring loci of Godâs revelation.â
Drawing on his experience as a pastor in Asia, particularly in India, Cardinal Neri Ferrão acknowledged that families had changed in their identity, nature, and composition, with smaller households, new forms of cohabitation, and interreligious marriages.
Families were increasingly on the move, and many faced economic insecurity, poverty, unemployment, and uncertainty about the future.
âChristian families in many parts of India and Asia,â the Cardinal stressed, âmust also live amid growing religious polarisation and hostility, making the public expression and transmission of faith increasingly difficult.â
Yet, these families also offered the Church beauty through their care for children, the elderly, the sick, and vulnerable people. Even amid poverty and uncertainty, the Cardinal explained, âour families continue to create positive spaces for joy and hope.â
Following the publication of Amoris laetitia , he recalled, the Churches in India and across Asia âlistened first to families,â and that listening âshaped how we walk with them. We now see marriage preparation as the start of a lifelong journey, offer spiritual renewal and counselling to couples and children, and keep forming families and lay leaders over time.â
He stressed that pastoral ministry needed to move âfrom mission to families to mission among families.â Families were not simply recipients of assistance but, in his words, âthe Church's partners in mission.â
Cardinal Neri Ferrão concluded by recounting the experience of a priest who had begun family ministry in his parish not with a program, but by visiting a family experiencing underlying difficulties in communication between the parents and between them and their children. It had begun with âa conversation and a willingness to listen.â
The second speaker, Vincenzo Rosito, Professor of the History and Culture of Family Institutions at the Pontifical Lateran University and Vice Dean of the Pontifical John Paul II Theological Institute for Marriage and Family Sciences, summed up his address with questions to guide participantsâ synodal discernment.
He began with an invitation inspired by Pope Leo XIVâs reflections in the encyclical Magnifica humanitas : âLet each of us be mindful of the relationships we build within our own families and within the Church.â
Professor Rosito stressed that âfamily practices, in fact, help us to understand how churches and families learn from one another. Both the Church and the family, in fact, learn through the practices of their daily lives.â
He then offered a question for participants to consider as a father, mother, theologian, or pastor: âAm I able to recognise and share with others at least one new thing that I have learnt to do, or to do differently, in recent years of my family or pastoral life?â
Changes in family life, Prof. Rosito explained, âare not problemsâ but âhuman activities.â Recalling Amoris laetitia , he presented them as an opportunity, as concrete processes âin which individuals and families act, react, learn and develop new resources.â
âConsider, for example,â the political philosopher continued, âhow the use of new digital technologies is transforming the daily habits of families and the way children are brought up.â
The family and the Church, Prof. Rosito continued, âlearn together through change.â He drew on the Gospel image of Jesus, Joseph, and Maryâs flight into Egypt.
He noted that today, âdrawing on the experiences of refugee and migrant families, some Christian communities are re-establishing themselves as ârefuge churchesââ for those arriving in a new land or making a long journey.
He also addressed the tragedy of violence shared by many families: âThe insecurity stemming from social and political violence is a worrying reality that many Churches must deal with today, in their daily lives.â Such insecurity, he warned, could âeven devour family bonds and church relationships themselves.â
Josephâs dream was also part of the experience of this flight.
âTo dream, to imagine new forms for the Church,â Prof. Rosito concluded, âalso means renewing what we already do. To imagine the Church means being willing to learn from one another, whilst we are transformed together, as churches and as families.â
His final question for discernment was therefore: âWhat do we need, amidst the light and shadow of today, to learn and imagine new ways of being a family and new ways of being the Church?â

articles.title_orig: Italy approves elections overhaul as opposition accuse Meloni of 'scam' law
articles.title_zh: Italy approves elections overhaul as opposition accuse Meloni of 'scam' law
articles.content_orig:
Italy's parliament has approved fiercely contested changes to the country's electoral system championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ahead of elections due next year.
Lawmakers voted 227 to 164 in favour of moving to a fully proportional system, which Meloni has argued will boost the chance of clear winners and more stable government.
Opposition parties say her right-wing coalition has designed the proposals to improve its chance of retaining power and, in a heated debate on Thursday, accused it of pushing through the "fraudulent" reform to flout democracy.
Meloni had warned she could resign and trigger an early election if the plans were rejected, with the secret ballot seen as a test of her authority.
Meloni's coalition has overseen a rare period of political stability for Italy since her election in 2022, and last month her government became the country's longest-running since World War Two.
The voting reform will see the country move away from its current hybrid voting system, in which about a third of members are chosen through a first-past-the-post vote and the rest through proportional representation.
Parties proposing to form a coalition will be required to put forward their joint candidate for prime minister, and their political programme, before any general election.
A party or coalition which emerges with the largest share of the votes - provided this exceeds 42% - will be awarded 105 additional seats in parliament (70 in the lower house and 35 in the senate), which could turn a narrow victory into a more comfortable majority.
Centre-left members held up signs with slogans including "No to the scam" and "fraudulent law" during a debate ahead of the vote, and accused the government of forcing through the new voting rules.
"Go ahead and change the electoral law, we will win in any case under any voting system," said Democratic Party (PD) leader Elly Schlein.
Five Star leader and former Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte told AFP news agency that the move was "a mess, a convoluted scheme, devised solely to find a formula to gain an advantage in the upcoming elections".
The proposals have also exposed tensions within the ranks of Meloni's coalition, too, with the Brothers of Italy (FdI) party and its allies, the far-right League and centre-right Forza Italia.
Analysts had predicted that Thursday's final vote was unlikely to fail - particularly given the number of lawmakers who would risk losing their eligibility for a parliamentary pension if their term was ended early as a result of the threatened snap election.
"To those who hoped to see the centre-right divided," Meloni wrote on social media after the vote, "today we respond with facts: we are united, cohesive, and determined to carry forward the commitments made to citizens."
She added: "We are introducing rules designed to promote the stability and parliamentary coherence of any government, regardless of its political colour."
Meloni's term officially comes to an end in October 2027, although she could bring elections forward to the spring.

articles.title_orig: Sports gambling seeps even deeper into Wall Street's world as hundreds of pro team ETFs emerge
articles.title_zh: Sports gambling seeps even deeper into Wall Street's world as hundreds of pro team ETFs emerge
articles.content_orig:
In 1989, all-time hits leader Pete Rose was banned from Major League Baseball for life because of his gambling activities. He wasn't reinstated until last year, months after his death in 2024.
Fast-forward to today, and Pete Rose's gambling might seem like just another day on Wall Street as financial firms expand the ways fans can put money behind their teams, beyond a beer and a $15 hot dog.
You may soon be able to buy a ticker for your favorite hockey team, and it isn't a stake in the franchise. Multiple asset managers have filed to launch dozens of ETFs, one for every NHL team, with MLB baseball team funds filed as well, all built on new futures contracts that track a team's season statistics. None has begun trading but in all, hundreds of ETFs that track the single-season performance of one professional team across a mix of statistical categories have been filed at the SEC for approval.
Some finance experts see the development as lacking any nuance whatsoever.
"The line between gambling and investing has not simply been blurred, it has been erased," said Robert Johnson, a professor of finance at Creighton University.
Among fund companies getting in on the novel trend are VolatilityShares , LeagueShares, Roundhill Investments , and Rex Financial .
None of the four companies responded to requests for comment. Asset managers typically cannot publicly comment during the period between when funds are filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission for approval and when they become effective, if approved.
Rex, a Miami-based ETF issuer, announced Sept. 21 that it was launching Alpha Sports Holdings, a new subsidiary built to turn team performance into exchange-traded funds. REX has filed with the SEC for BaseballShares and HockeyShares, suites of ETFs that would track Major League Baseball and National Hockey League teams through futures contracts that CME Group, the derivatives exchange, lists on indexes built by FutureSports, an index company. The underlying CME futures , which began trading for NHL teams in late September, need to first establish a trading history. MLB team futures are scheduled to launch on the CME on Oct. 12.
Each team's index opens the season at a set number and moves as the team racks up statistics, including runs scored, stolen bases and strikeouts for baseball, then resets in the offseason.
"The sports industry generates hundreds of billions of dollars a year, but there has never been a liquid, transparent investment product tied directly to what happens in live games," said Greg King, CEO of Alpha Sports, in a press release. "Alpha Sports exists to build that product for passionate investors who want to participate in the fortunes of their favorite teams."
Johnson, though, said the sports-themed ETFs are far more gaming than investing.
"I thought that the ETF world had jumped the shark with the introduction of the 2X and 3X leveraged and inverse ETFs. In my mind these were simply vehicles for short term speculators. But, at least these vehicles were based upon assets. The new structures — and I call them structures, not assets — are simply gambling dressed up as investing," Johnson said.
In fact, the proposed team ETFs include in some cases leveraged versions of trades on single-team performance.
The boom in prediction markets is already blurring the lines between sports wagering and market trading, with regulatory battles intensifying over the distinction — CNBC reported on Thursday that the NFL is pushing for prediction markets to be regulated by state gambling authorities. Unlike prediction markets contracts, the sports team ETFs are tracking futures off an index rather than a single event (e.g. win or loss). But while structurally contracts in this market have a role to play for investors, in the case of sports performance, Johnson says the case is weak.
"They have societal value in that parties are able to hedge natural positions and transact with other speculators willing to bear that risk. This allows a more optimal allocation of risk," Johnson said.
But he added that is not the case when individual investors are making bets on the performance of sports teams they follow.
"There are no natural positions being hedged. In the aggregate, they destroy wealth," Johnson said.
Here's a look at other stories offering insight on ETFs for investors.
Alex Michalka, vice president of investment research at investing platform Wealthfront, said the case for investing in the performance of sports teams is nearly impossible to separate from gambling, since wagering on whether a sports team will win or lose does not facilitate an economic purpose that adds value to the world.
"That is not to say a legitimate economic use case is impossible, but most people will likely use these funds for the same reasons they place a sports bet, which is often to show loyalty to a team or simply for entertainment," Michalka said. "Just because sports betting has an ETF wrapper, it does not change the risk associated with it," Michalka added.
Futures have long been used for hedging, and the CME contracts and FutureSports may be ways for sponsors, broadcasters, insurers and arena vendors to potentially hedge exposure against assets and liabilities. Conceptually, that's similar to an airline hedging fuel prices or an insurer hedging extreme weather risks. But in actuality, that does not apply to the vast majority of investors when it comes to these specific sports investments.
"Sports as an asset class exists, but for a few very select people out there," said Todd Sohn, chief ETF strategist at Baird Strategas. "I'm unsure if 'democratizing' really makes sense here," he said.
He added there are also many risks when it comes to novel ETFs like these with so few buyers in the market with a justifiable economic reason to trade them, risks that range from liquidity to price discovery and manipulation. Insider trading around injuries, trades, and coaching changes; and illiquidity in the investments during the offseason, up to four months of no activity, though trades and free agency can impact outlook, are among them. There should also be the expectations for wide bid/ask spreads and market imbalances with "fan enthusiasm driving prices and no commercial hedgers," Baird Strategas wrote in a preliminary analysis.
Despite the risks, all of which are covered in risk disclosures within these ETFs' prospectuses, Nate Geraci, an ETF expert and president of NovaDius Wealth Management, expects them to be approved by the SEC. Assuming the futures contracts "function properly, and establish sufficient liquidity, I don't see a regulatory reason why the SEC wouldn't approve the ETFs. CME-traded futures held in an ETF wrapper certainly aren't novel, though it's entirely possible the SEC could attempt to classify these sports-focused ETFs as such," he said.
The SEC is currently in the midst of a rulemaking proposal and public comment period covering "novel" ETFs, a move the regulator made after ETF companies filed for prediction markets ETFs.
Geraci is not surprised that ETF issuers are chasing the concept. "It's somewhat ironic that ETFs began as a way to offer low-cost, broad-based exposure to the market and have morphed in recent years into expensive, narrowly focused speculation vehicles. That said, it's a tale as old as time in asset management, where fund issuers rush to package and sell whatever is capturing investors' attention," he said.
Evan Mills, a financial advisor at Scholar Advising, an independent fee-only advisory firm, said it is important to understand the difference between owning a productive asset and making a bet on an outcome.
"If you're buying stock in a business, that stock is tied to revenue, earnings, and cash flow, so it appreciates based on that, as well as demand for the stock," Mills said. Bonds, meanwhile, include a contractual stream of payments, and that's how you make money off them.

articles.title_orig: South Korea to recall its ambassador to Ukraine over North Korean POW dispute
articles.title_zh: South Korea to recall its ambassador to Ukraine over North Korean POW dispute
articles.content_orig:
FILE - Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at United Nations headquarters, on Sept. 23, 2026. Seth Wenig/AP hide caption
SEOUL, South Korea — South Korea said Thursday it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, stepping up its protest against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recent revelation of a supposedly secret transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.
The South Korean announcement came days after its President Lee Jae Myung threatened to take unspecified punitive steps if Ukraine refuses to apologize over the revelation.
South Korea's Foreign Ministry didn't say when the ambassador, Park Hee-chang, will be brought back home. A ministry statement said that South Korea will continue consultations with Ukraine, adding it hopes the dispute between the two countries would be resolved smoothly.
South Korea and Ukraine became embroiled in a diplomatic row after Zelenskyy spoke about the transfer of the North Korean soldiers during his U.N. speech on Sept. 23. South Korea has accused Ukraine of violating a nondisclosure agreement on their transfer in mid-September, but Kyiv has denied agreeing to such a deal.
The soldiers were among thousands of North Korean troops deployed to support Russia's war against Ukraine. Since their capture in early 2025, the soldiers had expressed their desires to resettle in South Korea, because they could face persecution if repatriated home. South Korea had said it would accept them, because it legally regards the North as part of its territory and has a policy of accepting and financially supporting North Korean defectors.
South Korean officials said the non-disclosure agreement was made because they were concerned about the safety of the North Korean soldiers and their relatives in the North. But many experts say South Korea's liberal government likely also worries the disclosure of their arrival may hurt its efforts to improve ties with North Korea.
North Korea's state media hasn't commented on the soldiers' transfer. But the North previously reacted with fury to major defections of its citizens, accusing South Korea of kidnapping them. North Korea has shunned any talks with South Korea and the U.S. and focused on bolstering its nuclear program since 2019.
It's unclear what other steps South Korea would take. Experts say maintaining good relations with Ukraine is in South Korean national interests because Kyiv could provide Seoul with intelligence about North Korea's expanding cooperation with Russia and its battlefield experiences. They say cooperation with Ukraine is important for South Korea's partnerships with many Western countries supporting Ukraine over the war.
Observers say Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of the North Korean POWs to expose the danger of North Korea's military support to Russia as a way to win more international assistance.
South Korea has provided $445 million in humanitarian assistance to Ukraine since 2022. In July, Lee pledged $100 million in aid to Ukraine in a meeting with Zelenskyy,

articles.title_orig: Tanker hit by multiple projectiles in Gulf off Qatar, maritime agency says
articles.title_zh: Tanker hit by multiple projectiles in Gulf off Qatar, maritime agency says
articles.content_orig:
A tanker has been struck by "multiple projectiles" north of Qatar in the Gulf, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.
The incident - a rare attack deep inside the Gulf - happened 51 nautical miles (94km) from Madinat al-Shamal with casualties reported, the UKMTO said.
Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel as the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged oil and chemical tanker Acers. On Saturday it was reported as sailing towards the Strait of Hormuz waterway, which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.
Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the region since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.
At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 93 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization (IMO).
The IMO said the last incident that resulted in casualties was on 9 September, when two sailors were killed in an attack on the Panama-flagged tanker El Gaia in the Strait of Hormuz, just north of Oman's Musandam peninsula.
This is also the first reported attack on a ship this far west of the Strait of Hormuz since that same day, according to Martin Kelly, head of advisory at EOS Risk Group.
Also on Thursday, Vanguard amended an earlier report that had said there was a fire on board another tanker in the Gulf of Oman, about 40km east of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates.
The company clarified that there were no indications a fire occurred on the vessel, which it had identified as the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalkut.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Tehran's missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
Over the past two weeks, crude exports through the waterway have averaged 12 million barrels per day (bpd), which is around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler.

articles.title_orig: Going analog in algorithmic world
articles.title_zh: Going analog in algorithmic world
articles.content_orig:
Abby Brown, a 22-year-old crafter, finds Pinterest to be “AI slop.”
She recalls scrolling through the social media platform for inspiration in the past, but now she’s disenchanted by the surge of AI-generated images. It has turned her off from spending time online. Brown now finds herself reaching for her knitting needles.
“It makes me value handmade work more because I know a person spent a considerable amount of time making it,” she says.
Brown is part of a wave of young people who are starting to embrace analog hobbies—from knitting and pottery to film photography and risograph printing—as technology, artificial intelligence in particular, becomes increasingly ingrained in everyday life. Across Rochester, artists, business owners, and hobbyists say the appeal of analog isn’t nostalgia, but the ability to slow down and physically create something.
For many, it starts with what AI can’t offer: the meaning that comes from making something by hand.
Shelby Przybylek, owner of Little Button Craft, has witnessed that desire for meaningful art firsthand.
Over the last few years, she watched younger customers flock to crafting meetups, where they knit, crochet, or do other types of fiber arts.
Beyond simply seeking a human touch, Przybylek observes, many are turning to these tactile activities for their mental health benefits.
“People have really realized that it is a de-stressor, and you can really find some happiness when you’re making something with your hands,” she says.
Przybylek explains that bilateral integration —the brain’s ability to coordinate both sides of the body through efficient communication between the left and right hemispheres—sends chemicals to the brain that produce feelings of happiness and calm.
“When you’re working with your hands, it’s very calming—even if you make something that’s not perfect, it’s rewarding,” Przybylek says.
An increasingly popular way to create by hand is the art of pottery. A recently opened studio, Laurentide Clay , shows how pottery lets artists disconnect from screens. Terry O’Brien, the studio’s administrative coordinator, says he and other founders noticed a resurgence of interest in ceramics during and after the COVID-19 pandemic.
“There is something about being isolated and online that can feel a bit unnatural, at least to me,” he told the Beacon recently. He describes it as a question of offsetting an increasingly digital lifestyle with a craft that requires total focus. “I think it’s just establishing a balance in people’s lives.”
Kyle Lascelle, who oversees the studio’s educational programs, agreed with O’Brien, adding, “You have clay all over your hands, and so it’s difficult to be on your phone.”
The growing presence of algorithms has impacted people’s shopping habits. Sources for this article say many people are more intentional about who they support, encouraging them to seek out handmade products from real artists instead of machine-made graphics.
The desire for a more relaxed pace and to find analog ways to be creative isn’t limited to knitting, sewing, or even pottery. At Scott’s Photo, Tatiana Ariola has watched young people embrace another slower medium: film photography.
“The draw to film is the tangibility,” Ariola explains. “You can touch your negatives … they exist.”
Unlike digital photography, film photos cannot be readily altered.
“People are very much happier with film because it’s not edited,” explains Ariola. “You can always go back to the negative and know what was real.”
Unlike smartphone or digital cameras that can capture dozens of images in seconds, a roll of film offers just 24 or 36 exposures, making every photograph an intentional choice. In addition, many people today have grown accustomed to instant gratification, where photos are immediately available to see, edit, and post.
By using analog cameras, the photographer has to finish the roll of film, which then must be developed and the images printed.
“I think there’s a lot more intentionality (compared with) digital, where you can just spray and pray, take as many photos as you can, and hope that one comes out right,” Ariola says. “You can’t do that with film.”
Finding joy in the irregularities is what makes analog hobbies special.
“When you see an imperfection, you know (that) definitely a human made this,” says Brown.
For Evan Bobrow at Rathaus Press, a risograph printing business, imperfections are what make a risograph, a combination of screen printing and photocopying, distinct from other printing methods.
“​​There will always be misregistration,” Bobrow says. “There will always be some level of smudging or different levels of coverage, and yeah, a lot of people are interested in that. That it makes it feel like more of a handmade object.”
He believes the desire to go analog is human and tactile.
“I think knowing that whoever made something made a really intentional choice to make it physical can make that connection feel more special,” he says.
Brown says knitting gives her an intentional reason to step away from screens that increasingly overpower work, school, and social life.
At the same time, social media has helped bring more attention to those crafts.
“I think it’s helped introduce more people to film photography, and to get people information to improve their photography, and it’s also a platform to share your work,” Ariola says.
“I think that it’s very good for the people who are trying to get into crafting to see what the process is like before they have to buy all of the products and try on their own,” she says.
For Brown, crafting isn’t just something to do alone. It’s become a way to meet people outside of work, school, and social media. After graduating from Rochester Institute of Technology, she’s been searching for third spaces —places beyond home and work where people can create genuine communities and connections.
Little Button Craft hosts Fiber Nights at Abundance Food Co-op every Wednesday (except the second Wednesday of the month) from 6-8 p.m. Przybylek hopes that attendees will use those weekly meetings to de-stress and be among their crafty peers. Alongside Fiber Nights, she wants to keep offering low-cost courses for people seeking to get into art.
“I think it’s being brave and creating that third space for people, because they will come, they will very much come,” she says.
Przybylek has noticed that some of those who religiously attend Fiber Night events have created their own friend groups and then meet up to do crafts together.
“They’re forming this beautiful friendship that started with crafting,” she says.
Scott’s Photo is aiming to become a third space for film photographers, a community hub where people can learn from each other and share their work, Ariola says. The store has been hosting monthly photo walks at various locations in the city and beyond.
Rathaus Press has open hours for creatives to come in and use its facilities. Bobrow describes the setting as a collaborative space for people to create art.
“Art (can) be something that’s very personal, but I think it’s also really important for it to be a communal experience,” he says.
Jacob Dambra, the community coordinator at Laurentide Clay, has noticed that various ceramic studios in Rochester provide a breeding ground for communities to form.
“So many people I know through ceramics have built most of their social network,” says Dambra. “It almost doesn’t make sense to do (ceramics) by yourself.”
This shift to analog isn’t unique to Rochester; it reflects what appears to be a national trend that has emerged in recent years, fed by a growing dissatisfaction with technology.
In a 2023 Harris Poll , a majority of Gen Z and millennial respondents (58% each) said they believe new technologies are more likely to drive people apart than bring them together. At a Google Cloud event on Thursday, the company announced it’s bringing its Gemini AI into the agentic age, with the launch of a unified agent that can not only answer questions but also get things done on the user’s behalf, all from a single interface.
The move comes as AI tools have been moving beyond being just conversational experiences to those that can take ownership of assigned tasks, generate code, schedule meetings, book appointments and travel, and more. It also follows the rise of consumer-facing agents like Meta’s Muse and those that operate over messaging, like Instinct and others, as well as the recent debut of ChatGPT’s Dots.
The company still has a good shot at achieving scale for its agentic efforts: as Google CEO Sundar Pichai pointed out at the event’s start, Gemini today has over 1 billion monthly active users. He also noted that nearly 90% of Fortune 100 businesses now use Gemini Enterprise at work.
Given Gemini’s adoption in the corporate world, Google will initially focus on bringing the agent to businesses before later rolling it out to consumers.
According to Pichai, this will allow the company to solve the “harder problems around security, scale, and performance,” which come with launching powerful agents such as these.
Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, explained that the new agent can be given “objectives, not just instructions.” That means it’s able to plan the work, use custom skills and tools, and connect to businesses’ internal systems to accomplish its goals.
By default, the AI will pick the best model to complete the task, but users can also take over to choose a model — including those from third parties, starting with Anthropic’s Claude models. Google said that it will expand the model picker to include open source models and other private models in the future.
The request can include attachments, like files, folders, or other projects designed for specific workstreams, like those that combine files and skills. The agent can connect to the business’s data and systems, like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, Confluence, Git, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, and others.
It can also connect and work securely with any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside the company’s network.
Users can keep track of what Gemini is doing from a “tasks inbox” interface, where they can see Gemini’s thinking process, delegation of tasks to subagents, loading of special skills, code, and progress.
Notably, the AI will have its own Workspace account, as if it’s just another coworker. That means it has its own email address and its own context, Google said. It knows who at the company is on what team, their time zones, who needs to approve items, what’s on people’s calendars, and more. Users can call the agent by tagging it, emailing it, sharing with it, or adding it to a group chat. As it takes action, it writes an audit trail attributed to the agent, instead of a person.
The agent will be accessible from iOS and Android mobile devices, Windows and Mac desktops, the command line interface, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, ServiceNow, and Slack.
The agent’s early testers included sportswear brand On, Shopify, and PayPal, and noted that Gemini Enterprise customers include large businesses like BNP Paribas, Bradesco, Merck, Orange Spain, Santee Cooper, SOMPO, Ulta Beauty, and Wesfarmers.
Google said new flexible spending options, including multi-model orchestration, smart routing, and real-time spend caps, will help businesses keep their enterprise AI costs under better control.

Collaboration creates unmatched capabilities in biopharma industry for real world data generation and insights for market access strategy
CHICAGO , Oct. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- EVERSANA , a leading provider of technology enabled, modern commercialization services to the biopharmaceutical industry, today announced a strategic partnership with Pulse Infoframe, a leader in real-world evidence (RWE) generation and intelligence. Through the partnership, EVERSANA will pair its end-to-end commercialization, market access and health economics and outcomes research (HEOR) expertise with Pulse Infoframe's proprietary RWE platform and established evidence-generation capabilities, creating a single, continuous evidence engine for pharmaceutical and medical device companies.
The partnership spans the full arc of evidence generation: global site-network and feasibility assessments, registry and natural history study design, and direct data capture from sites and patients, followed by HTA-grade reporting, global value dossiers, and reimbursement strategy. By designing studies to serve regulators, HTA bodies, and commercial teams alike, EVERSANA and Pulse Infoframe help clients carry a single evidence base from first patient enrolled through launch and beyond.
"Real-world evidence has never been more critical as pharmaceutical companies work to develop the best strategies to bring innovative therapies to patients," said Mark Thierer, Chief Executive Officer, EVERSANA. "By pairing our deep commercial and health economics expertise with Pulse Infoframe's robust registry expertise in complex conditions, including rare disease and oncology, we can bring unmatched solutions to customers to help improve market access."
The partnership offers pharmaceutical and medical device manufacturers a seamless solution for evidence generation from study design and global site-network assessments to sophisticated external control arm methods and Health Technology Assessment (HTA)-grade reporting. By uniting complementary strengths, the collaboration delivers compounding gains in efficiency, data quality, and global scale.
"Our platform was built to generate regulatory-grade evidence directly from sites and patients," said Femida Gwadry-Sridhar (PhD), Chief Executive Officer, Pulse Infoframe. "Working with EVERSANA connects that evidence to the regulatory, reimbursement, and commercial decisions it needs to support, at global scale."
The partnership will be highlighted by EVERSANA and Pulse Infoframe at ISPOR Europe 2026, November 8-11 in Vienna, Austria.
About EVERSANA ® EVERSANA ® is the leading independent provider of global services to the life sciences industry. The company's integrated solutions are rooted in the patient experience and span all stages of the product life cycle to deliver long-term, sustainable value for patients, prescribers, channel partners, and payers. The company serves more than 650 organizations, including innovative start-ups and established pharmaceutical companies, to advance life sciences solutions for a healthier world. To learn more about EVERSANA, visit eversana.com .
About Pulse Infoframe Pulse Infoframe is a leading real-world data and evidence generation partner that provides services to clients in the life sciences and healthcare sectors. The company owns and operates its real-world evidence platform, with expertise in registries, natural history studies, and the ability to generate regulatory-grade data directly from sites and patients.

articles.title_orig: The World is His Oyster
articles.title_zh: The World is His Oyster
articles.content_orig:
October 8, 2026 | Claire Hall
Seafood entrepreneur Keegan Jalbert is developing a new approach to oyster feed
Graduate student Keegan Jalbert, left, and his brother-in-law Bryan Zambrano are pictured on a boat as they visit an aquaculture farm in Ecuador, where they discussed feed trials using AccessFlora's proprietary omega-3 feed. Jalbert's startup is one of the finalists in next week's Wolff New Venture Competition (UConn Today).
Graduate student Keegan Jalbert ’23 (CLAS) ’27 MS (CAHNR) has always been interested in agriculture, food, and innovation. Today he is finding new ways to grow oysters and share his love of seafood with customers who live far from the ocean.
Jalbert is the founder of AccessFlora , a sustainable aquaculture company with a proprietary omega-3 aquafeed for raising oysters in purified water at a hatchery. The outcome is a larger and healthier shellfish that isn’t confined to the coast nor dependent upon favorable ocean conditions.
“I think what keeps me going as an entrepreneur is that this work is very fun,’’ says Jalbert, who is pursuing a master’s degree in nutritional science. “My greatest motivation is the impact on how we source omega-3s as a critical nutrient for our human health and for agriculture. What’s helped me so much with the startup is that I love my work, and because of it I’ve developed great personal connections.’’
Startup to Compete in Wolff New Venture Championship
AccessFlora is one of five UConn-affiliated startups participating in the Wolff New Venture Competition next Tuesday, Oct. 13, at Pratt & Whitney Stadium at Rentschler Field in East Hartford.
The competition, now in its 11th year, is hosted by the Connecticut Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation (CCEI) . The event will include awards of more than $150,000, including a $40,000 grand prize for the first-place finisher. Jalbert says whatever money AccessFlora wins will help ramp up production.
“In terms of shellfish farming, yes, what we’re doing is revolutionary,’’ Jalbert says. “Shellfish are not raised in land-based aquaculture because the omega-3 feed would be too expensive. On one hand, that makes shellfish really great, because they can grow out in the ocean without being fed and they are great for the environment. But on the other hand, this cultivation method takes a long time, it is labor intensive, and it is vulnerable to unpredictable ocean conditions. While our technology will not replace traditional shellfish farming, it does provide a highly resilient and quick way to raise oysters, independent of ocean access, allowing this to be done inland.’’
“The way that this technology works is that we have a healthy microalgae that we use to convert vinegar into omega-3 in controlled conditions, kind of like yeast turns sugars into alcohol,’’ Jalbert says. “This gives us a clean DHA omega-3, the nutrient that makes seafood such an important part in our diet.’’
But that’s just one step for the company.
“Our longer-term plan is for this to not just be raising oysters, but to be serving as an omega-3 source in enriched/fortified plant-based foods,’’ Jalbert says. “This is because that is a large market that our technology is really well suited for, especially now that the majority of U.S. population is deficient in omega-3.’’
Jalbert Brings Extensive Experience to His Work
Jalbert’s startup won the 2025 Innovation Quest competition at UConn and a $15,000 grand prize. He has partnered with professor Mingyu Qiao, in the Department of Nutritional Sciences in the College of Agriculture, Health and Natural Resources, who is a leader and innovator in sustainable food systems.
In addition, Jalbert took advantage of UConn’s co-op program and worked with both the Boston Beer Company, in new product development, and as a microbiology intern at the U.S. Department of Energy. Through exchange programs, he has learned about shellfish aquaculture in Melbourne, Australia, Manabi, Ecuador, as well as here in Connecticut.
Summer Accelerator: ‘I Must Have Learned 100 Things’
Part of Jalbert’s entrepreneurial journey included attending CCEI’s eight-week Summer Accelerator, which offers promising startups $15,000 in non-dilutive funding, mentorship, access to masterclasses and workshops, and pro-bono legal, accounting, marketing, product development, and banking services.
“Summer Accelerator is like a summer camp for startups,’’ Jalbert says. “It packs a lot into eight weeks. This summer we were testing how we can distribute our omega-3 product and learning the cost structures and economics of getting product to customers. I must have learned 100 things during Summer Accelerator, but the biggest thing was unit economics and cost structure of bringing the product to market.’’
With the oyster feed gaining traction, AccessFlora is focusing on educating people on the seafood nutrient. Jalbert just hired his first employee to work on business outreach. “We are in real talks with restaurants and agricultural experts,’’ he says.
AccessFlora also manages a food trailer, called Reef-to-Table, which caters weddings and other events. Although that isn’t the primary focus of the business, it is a terrific outlet for Jalbert.
“It’s a good way of having direct interactions with consumers. I enjoy it so much,’’ he says. “I have to be conscience of my time commitments, but if it could be my weekend hobby, I’d do it. The raw bar business is a ton of fun and already profitable.”
The Wolff New Venture Competition will be held on Tuesday (Oct. 13) at Pratt and Whitney Stadium at Rentschler Field in East Hartford from 5 to 9 p.m. The event is free to attend and all are welcome. Pre-registration is required at https://luma.com/i2690pqa .
The Wolff New Venture Competition is supported by the generosity of the Wolff Family as well as wiggin(x), Fiondella, Milone & LaSaracina LLP, Sardilli Produce and Dairy Co., Prime Materials Recovery Inc., Big Bang, Baystate Financial, Webster Bank, Mark and Jamie Summers, Putnam Plastics, Eric Marziali, Bob and Linda Delisle, Dick and Carol Stewart and Event Resources.

articles.title_orig: Alabama’s Prehistoric Past: Fossils Reveal a World That Existed Millions of Years Ago
articles.title_zh: Alabama’s Prehistoric Past: Fossils Reveal a World That Existed Millions of Years Ago
articles.content_orig:
by Brian White, Ashonti Ford
When most people think about dinosaur fossils, they may picture the wide-open landscapes of Montana, Wyoming or the Dakotas.
But some of the most significant fossil discoveries in the country are much closer to home — right here in Alabama.
Inside the Birmingham Mcwane Center, thousands of fossils are stored just feet away from visitors, offering a glimpse into an Alabama that existed long before the state — or even humans — were here.
Behind collection-room doors, row after row of cabinets hold bones, teeth and other remnants of life dating back more than half a billion years.
June Ebersole, director of collections at McWane Science Center, oversees about half a million specimens, including fossils found nowhere else in the world.
“A lot of people think you have to go out west to find fossils,” Ebersole said. “But what my research is showing is that Alabama, by far, is the number one state in the U.S. in terms of paleo-biodiversity.”
The collection spans an extraordinary stretch of time.
“We have fossils here that are over 500 million years old, to some that are just from the Ice Age, only 12,000 to 14,000 years old, and everything in between,” Ebersole said. “We have so many fossils here, I’m discovering new species all the time.”
Among the most remarkable specimens is one that helped change what scientists knew about dinosaurs in the eastern United States.
Ebersole opens a drawer containing the remains of Eotrachodon orientalis, a newly identified species of duck-billed dinosaur.
The fossils may look like a pile of bones to the untrained eye, but together they represent the most complete dinosaur ever found in the eastern half of the United States, with about 60% of its skeleton recovered.
And the discovery was made not in a remote western desert, but in Montgomery County.
“It’s from Montgomery County, right on the side of the creek, just outside the city limits,” Ebersole said. “This is the only one of this particular species in the world.”
The dinosaur is only part of Alabama’s prehistoric story.
The McWane collection also includes fossils of sharks, turtles and birds, along with a 315-million-year-old dragonfly wing discovered in Walker County.
Thousands of fossil shark teeth fill drawers inside the collection, including one massive collection from the time of the dinosaurs.
“It is literally — here’s 10,000 fossil goblin shark teeth,” Ebersole said. “It’s one of the biggest collections of these on the planet.”
Most visitors to the science center will see only a fraction of the collection.
But behind the scenes, scientists continue studying the specimens and making discoveries that help reconstruct the world that existed beneath Alabama millions of years ago.
Long before 250 years of American history, Alabama was already writing a story of its own — one measured not in centuries, but in hundreds of millions of years.
And today, pieces of that ancient story remain carefully preserved, waiting to reveal what Alabama looked like long before any of us arrived.

articles.title_orig: Why California could ban a popular feature for high-end kitchen remodels
articles.title_zh: Why California could ban a popular feature for high-end kitchen remodels
articles.content_orig:
Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.
One of the most popular types of kitchen countertops will soon face a ban in California due to its link to a serious lung disease, The New York Times reported this week, citing an emergency regulation that is expected to be passed by the state later this month.
The ban will target quartz countertops that have more than 1% of crystalline silica, a naturally occurring mineral that is found in stone and other materials.
When crystalline silica is cut or drilled through, it creates dust. If that dust is inhaled, it can cause numerous health conditions, including silicosis, an incurable lung disease, according to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration . The disease can be fatal, but symptoms do not typically occur directly after an exposure to crystalline silica dust. Instead, it can take 15 to 20 years after exposure before someone is diagnosed with the disease.
According to the National Cancer Institute , exposure to the harmful dust most often occurs in occupational settings, making those who work with the material every day the most at risk. An estimated 2.3 million US workers are exposed to silica through work.
Silicosis is similar to asbestosis, which is caused by exposure to asbestos , a now-banned building material that was once widely used throughout the US.
In addition to silicosis, exposure to crystalline silica dust can cause an increased risk of developing lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and kidney disease, according to OSHA. As of now, quartz countertops are used in every state in the US. California would be the first to implement a ban.
It’s unclear whether other states will follow California, but as of now, Australia is the only country in the world with a quartz ban, which took effect in 2024 .
Regardless, quartz remains an extremely popular option throughout the world, with some estimates putting the global quartz market at $14.8 billion as of 2026.
Other countertop options include soapstone or granite. Although other stone countertops can still have crystalline silica in them, quartz typically has the highest content, which is why it has been the most scrutinized.
To stay away from crystalline silica entirely, a wooden countertop is one of the best alternatives.

articles.title_orig: Oil prices jump on tanker attacks and slowing flows through Strait of Hormuz
articles.title_zh: Oil prices jump on tanker attacks and slowing flows through Strait of Hormuz
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices rose sharply Thursday, as Iran ramped up its attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz and Hurricane Isaias threatened U.S. offshore production in the Gulf of Mexico.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, gained 3.8% to $104.04 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures advanced 3.4% at $91.28.
Nine tankers have come under attack in and around Hormuz over the past week, jeopardizing the recent recovery in crude oil flows through the strait
Oil prices backed off session highs after President Donald Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the November midterm elections. NBC News, citing unnamed sources, reported earlier that Trump and his national security team were considering renewing strikes in the coming weeks.
Some 9.5 million barrels per day exited Hormuz during the week ended Tuesday, about 30% below normal levels before the Iran war, according to Kpler data. Crude flows from the Middle East, including pipeline workarounds, stood at 16.4 million bpd which is nearly equivalent to prewar levels.
In the Gulf of Mexico, oil companies have shut in about 500,000 bpd, or 25% of offshore production in the region, as Hurricane Isaias churns toward the coasts of Alabama, Mississippi and the Florida panhandle.
Tensions are sharply escalating in the Middle East. Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen fired missiles at airports in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and the city of Abha on Tuesday and Wednesday. Three people died and 36 were injured, according to the state-owned media outlet Al Arabiya.
The Saudis intercepted another volley of ballistic missiles fired Thursday at Riyadh and Khamis Mushait, a spokesperson for the kingdom's military said.
"While flows from the region have largely normalized, the need for US navy escorts, increased costs and logistical frictions and constant risk of being attacked call into question the longer-term feasibility of the flows," said Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities.
"This ultimately warrants a sticky risk premium to remain in pricing," McKay told clients in a Thursday note.

articles.title_orig: He planned to become a philosopher. Then he found New Orleans’ startup world.
articles.title_zh: He planned to become a philosopher. Then he found New Orleans’ startup world.
articles.content_orig:
In college, Andrew Albert imagined a career in academia. He’d get global experience, earn a PhD in philosophy, come back to start a think tank in New Orleans and shape public policy in his hometown.
In the end, he did build a career that contributes to New Orleans — but in the city’s startup ecosystem.
He’s now programs director at the Idea Village , where he leads the team responsible for its accelerators, thought leadership and marketing and communications.
“What does it mean to be Black in the South and wrestle with institutions and power?”
His path there included working at New Orleans software startup Lucid during its $60 million Series B, before it became New Orleans’ first tech unicorn. He went on to support founders through Venture for America , co-found River Basin Distillery and later launch Exclave Spirits .
In this edition of How I Got Here , Albert talked about trading academia for startups, the job he considers his “working MBA” and what people hoping to build companies should know.
This Q&A has been edited for length and clarity.
Being Black from New Orleans, it was like: Go be a lawyer, go be a doctor. Those are the traditional pathways. So I started my undergrad career at Loyola University New Orleans as a bio major. I was like, “Oh, cool. I guess I’ll go become a doctor.”
But because Loyola is a Jesuit university, all freshmen take Intro to Philosophy. I had a chem lab with no windows and fluorescent lights, and then I went to this philosophy class with these very heady questions. It was incredibly appealing.
I literally dropped everything within that semester and switched to philosophy.
A lot of my undergraduate career was spent studying dynamics of power, specifically racial power. What does it mean to be Black in the South and wrestle with institutions and power? How might you see yourself in the world?
I had every intention of being a full-time academic. I had an amazing mentor who suggested I get a master’s degree first to figure out whether grad school was really what I wanted.
I’d had a Fulbright experience in the UK and fell in love with London. I was also a super nerd. You hear the stories about James Baldwin and the intellectual expat, and I knew I wanted to do something abroad.
So I went to the London School of Economics to study philosophy and public policy.
I immediately got to grad school and was like, “I do not like this at all.”
Before that, my ambition was to get a PhD, make policy recommendations, yada yada yada, solve the world’s problems. That was my very naive educational journey.
I knew fairly quickly that my educational journey was going to stop at the master’s level. In retrospect, that was probably a great thing because it gave me time to reflect on what I actually wanted to do.
A core driver for me was: How might I participate within the city of New Orleans in some productive fashion? Originally, I thought it was policy. I realized I didn’t want to do that.
This was the golden age of startups, and I was living in East London, where there was a lot of buzz and excitement around them.
One option was Venture for America, a fellowship for recent grads who wanted to work at high-growth startups. I applied, got accepted and really put all my eggs in the “I’m working in New Orleans” basket.
Thinking back on it, I had this singular idea: Whatever the best company in the world is, that’s the company I’m going to work for.
Plan B was to do Plan A for me.
I was fortunate enough to land that role at Lucid.
My title was executive analyst, but I worked there essentially in a chief of staff role. I did everything from financial planning and analysis and board governance to designing a 35,000-sq.-ft.office space. If there was a job that needed to be done and there wasn’t a full-time hire to do it, it was my role.
My time at Lucid was very much my working MBA. We raised a $60 million Series B, which in New Orleans was a massive amount of capital. I got to work with bankers.
I remember the CEO at the time telling me, “The amount of access that you’re going to get here far surpasses what you’re supposed to have, and it is going to completely warp how you move through your profession.”
Then I pivoted away from operationally working in startups and went back to what I was interested in from school: economic development.
I ended up working for Venture for America. First, I was director of New Orleans, and then I became VP of venture growth, where I spent most of my time building our venture growth department, essentially the entrepreneurship department.
I helped design how we supported fellows and alumni on their entrepreneurial journeys, ran our accelerator and all of our entrepreneurial programming. It really was like 1-800-founder for the better part of six and a half years.
Around 2017 or 2018, I read the story of Nearest Green and Uncle Nearest Whiskey. I remember thinking, “God damn, why didn’t I come up with this? This is amazing.”
After those emotions went away, the next thing was: This is actually a global Black story that can and should be told. This isn’t just an American Black story.
That seed eventually became part of Exclave Spirits, which tells a broader story of how Black people have contributed to distilled spirits.
Actually building something changed how I work with founders. It’s the difference between theory and practice.
By building something, I was able to cut out the jargon and get to the foundational principles of what it means to build a business.
The hard part is being able to assess risk, anticipate things and make very tight resource decisions. You hear stories of investors pushing, pushing, pushing, and founders losing sight of why they got into it in the first place.
My approach is: I don’t know exactly what you’re going through. This shit is hard. It’s lonely. It’s winding. But I try to be the friendly voice saying, “All right, I know it’s hard, but keep pushing.”
Being perpetually curious is something you can develop and always work on.
Be comfortable with pivoting, because everything we put on a whiteboard sounds great to ourselves. The minute you take a step forward, you’re going to face something that forces you to change.
There’s the “fail fast” adage. I switch it to: Be able to pivot and rebound fast.
The other thing is to be very diligent with how you question your customers. You can build something great, something technologically ahead of everybody else. Awesome. But what I always go back to is: Will somebody give you money for it repeatedly?
If not, you kind of just have a science project, which is cool. But at the core of it, a business is: You create value that somebody pays you for.
And what’s the worst that could happen?
The cost of building is as low as it’s probably ever been. To the extent that you see a problem, see a challenge, take a shot. What’s the worst thing that’s going to happen?
The Big Table Institute is launching virtual programs that help mission-driven professionals, small business owners and entrepreneurs explore what’s possible.
New Orleans-based Geaux River raised $300,000 to expand wireless data collection, barge tracking and maritime defense tools on US waterways.
